Decision records

Each record explains one decision of the architecture: the situation, what we decided, what follows from it, what else we considered, and which checks enforce it.

How to give feedbackUse this page's comment button. Mention the section number shown next to each heading (for example §7), or select text and comment on it. Tapping a section number copies it, ready to paste into your comment.

ADR-0001: Modular monolith in one binary

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Bugaboo must be secure, fast and installable on Windows, Linux and WSL by people without operations experience. The scale target (500 people, 1 M issues) fits one machine.

Decision

Build one Rust binary containing the API, the embedded browser app, background jobs and the MCP server. Inside, use a hexagonal structure: a pure domain core (bb-core, bb-policy, bb-searchlang, bb-markdown), use cases (bb-app) that depend only on ports (traits), and adapters (bb-store, bb-files, bb-ai, bb-notify, bb-api, bb-mcp). Module boundaries are crates, and dependency rules are checked by cargo xtask check only ARCH-DEPS.

Consequences

  • One process, one security boundary, one thing to install, back up and update.
  • Use cases are testable with in-memory fakes; adapters are tested separately.
  • Scaling beyond one machine would need work later (accepted: not a 1.0 goal).

Alternatives considered

  • Microservices: more moving parts, more attack surface, harder installation. Rejected.
  • One big crate: faster to start, but boundaries erode and compile times grow. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-DEPS, ARCH-HTTP-EDGE, ARCH-MAP-SYNC, META-NEW-MODULE (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0002: HTTP stack: Tokio, axum, rustls

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

We need a mature async HTTP server with good middleware, HTTPS without system OpenSSL, and easy static builds for Windows and Linux.

Decision

Use tokio as the runtime, axum for routing and extractors, tower-http for compression, headers and limits, and rustls (with tokio-rustls) for TLS, using the ring crypto provider so static musl and Windows builds need no C toolchain beyond what Rust ships. instant-acme handles certificates from ACME.

Consequences

  • No OpenSSL dependency; memory-safe TLS.
  • axum extractors give one place to turn credentials into an actor.

Alternatives considered

  • actix-web: fine, but a smaller middleware ecosystem around tower.
  • aws-lc-rs provider: stronger FIPS story, but needs CMake/C for static builds; revisit if FIPS is ever required.

Enforced by

SEC-HEADERS, DEP-LICENSES (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0003: Databases: SQLite by default, PostgreSQL optional

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Installation must work with zero setup, but larger installations and the served model need a server database.

Decision

Support SQLite (bundled, WAL mode) and PostgreSQL 16+ through sqlx. Write queries with sea-query (bound through sea-query-sqlx) so one query definition produces both dialects. Define the schema and migrations once in Rust with the same query builder; both databases run the same migration list. Dialect-specific code is allowed only behind the bb-store port implementations and needs a comment explaining why.

Consequences

  • Every repository test runs against both databases in CI.
  • Some PostgreSQL features (for example row-level security) are not used in core paths; authorization stays in bb-policy anyway.
  • The served model uses PostgreSQL; self-hosted installations start with SQLite and can migrate with bugaboo migrate-to-postgres.

Alternatives considered

  • PostgreSQL only: simpler code, harder installation. Rejected for the default.
  • SeaORM: less control over generated SQL for permission predicates. Rejected.
  • Two hand-written migration folders: violates SSOT. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-SQL-EDGE, DATA-MIGRATIONS, ARCH-DB-PARITY (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0004: Authorization: one policy engine and Authorized

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04 · refined by ADR-0025

Context

Security is priority one. Permissions go down to single fields and single issues, and many entry points (UI, API, search, MCP, assistant, e-mail, webhooks, exports, live updates) must all obey them.

Decision

  • All decisions are made by bb-policy: permission catalogue, role assignments on the project tree with inheritance and explicit deny, field masks, visibility groups and token scopes.
  • Data leaves the domain only as Authorized<T>, whose constructor is private to bb-policy. It carries the field mask and applies it when serialized. Returning plain domain types from bb-app is a compile error at the API layer.
  • Searches get the actor's visibility predicates compiled into the same SQL query, and the parser only knows readable fields, so a hidden field looks exactly like an unknown one.
  • Outbound channels (notifications, webhooks, live updates, exports, assistant context) apply the receiver's mask.

Consequences

  • Forgetting a check is hard: the types don't line up.
  • A generated test matrix (roles × permissions × fields × entry points) runs on every build.
  • Per-request caching of evaluations keeps it fast.

Alternatives considered

  • Checks in each handler: easy to forget one. Rejected.
  • Database row-level security: PostgreSQL only, and field-level rules would still be needed in code. Rejected.
  • External policy engines (OPA, Cedar): another language and runtime to secure and ship; our model is fixed and well understood. Rejected for now; the catalogue could be exported to Cedar later.

Enforced by

ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY, ARCH-API-OUT, ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0005: Search language: one Rust crate, also in the browser

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

People need simple filter buttons and an advanced typed search, converting exactly into each other, with the same behavior in the browser and on the server, and without copying another vendor's language.

Decision

Write bb-searchlang: lexer, parser, syntax tree, canonical printer, checker and suggestions, with no I/O. Simple search edits the syntax tree; Advanced search edits text that parses into the same tree. Compile the crate to WebAssembly (bb-wasm) for instant highlighting, suggestions and error messages in the browser. The server compiles the tree to SQL in bb-store.

Consequences

  • One grammar (SSOT). Property test: parse(print(tree)) == tree.
  • WebAssembly adds download size; it's loaded only when search is first used, within its own WebAssembly budget in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml (amendment M5, decision 7).

Alternatives considered

  • A grammar written twice (Rust and TypeScript): drifts. Rejected.
  • Parser generators (pest, lalrpop): fine, but hand-written recursive descent gives better plain-language error messages. Decision left to the milestone, as long as the crate stays I/O-free.

Amendment M5: the words, the limits and what crosses the wire

The M5 proposals (M5-Q7, Q10) were accepted. Decided:

  1. The parser is written by hand (recursive descent), for plain-language messages and a small WebAssembly module. No parser generator.
  2. English words for the language (and, or, not, is, is not, contains, in last, sort by …). A field is written as on screen, as one word in lower camel case (assignedTo, statusGroup) (amended by decision 11: since D3 a field is written as the glossary names it, in lower case with spaces, assigned to; the one-word form is still read). The word of each built-in field is defined once, next to the field; an own field gets its word from its name by one rule, and a name that cannot be written as one word is written in quotes. The search text is the same in every language of the app, so a shared search works for everyone.
  3. The language holds filters and the order (sort by). How a search is shown (columns, widths, spacing, grouping) is not part of it; a saved search stores that beside the text (amended by ADR-0034, amendment "Spacing is the person's own": the spacing is the person's setting, and a saved search keeps no spacing).
  4. The canonical text is what travels: the address, the API and a saved search carry the text the printer writes; the tree never crosses the wire. The server parses and checks every search again and never relies on the browser's check.
  5. The checker is given the fields the person may read (the readable fields). A field outside that set is unknown: the same message, the same error code and no difference in time to a field that does not exist (QRY-05).
  6. Limits of the language (the parser and the checker enforce them): at most 50 filters (a list in (a, b) counts as many as it has values), within N steps at most 5 (M5-Q10), at most 5 keys in sort by, and a text of at most 4 096 bytes (a fix of the review of M5 WP-02: no work is done for a longer text). The time, page and rate limits are the server's (SEC-17, M5 WP-04).
  7. A module of its own (the lead): the search language is a WebAssembly module of its own, fetched when a search bar first opens, with its own budget in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml (set by M5 WP-02 from its measurement, at most 100 KB with Brotli). The shared budget of 150 KB was planned for Markdown and the search language; the wording of changes and notifications (M4 WP-13) took it, the module is at 145.6 KB, and a list should not fetch Markdown, nor an editor the search language. Each module keeps a budget of its own.
  8. How the module is made (M5 WP-02): the bindings are a crate of their own, bb-wasm-search, loaded by the package @bugaboo/wasm-search; bb-wasm keeps Markdown and the wording. The browser gives the tree and the readable fields as JSON, which the module reads with a reader that is generated from the Rust types (cargo xtask gen search-reader, held to the types by DOC-GENERATED): deriving Deserialize made the module bigger than its budget (116 KB with Brotli against 100 KB at most), and a reader written by hand would be a second definition of the tree. A tree that is read is held to the rules of a tree (a day of the calendar, an Issue ID by the rules of bb-core, a number in its shortest form, and and or of at least two items with none of their own kind inside; how deep a tree may be is the parser's rule (MAX_DEPTH), and a tree that is too deep has no text that reads back), and print of the module writes the canonical text of the tree it is given: whether that text reads back as the same tree is held by the tests (TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP) and, for every text that is saved or run, by the server (canonical_text and the check of the text it receives), not by the module. The reader is behind the feature browser of bb-searchlang, which only bb-wasm-search turns on: the server never reads a tree from outside. bb-searchlang depends on bb-core for the rules of an Issue ID and of a short name, so the browser and the server read an ID the same way (architecture §4, rule 1). Places in the answers are bytes of the UTF-8 text; the package turns them into places in the string. The check that a printed text reads back as the same tree (canonical_text) is the feature round-trip-guard of bb-searchlang: the server and the tests build with it, so a defect of the printer can never be saved or run, and the module of the browser builds without it, because the check costs about 7 KB of the module (its budget in perf-bundle.toml); everything the browser prints is sent to the server, which parses and checks it again, and no path of the browser depends on the check to refuse a text. Measured at 88.9 KB with Brotli at the server's quality; the budget line is in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml.

Enforced by: TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP (decisions 1 to 4, the printer and the parser), the tests of M5 WP-02 (decisions 5 and 6), SEC-MATRIX with the search entry point (decision 5 on the server), PERF-BUNDLE (decision 7).

  1. Values are written as the person sees them (the lead, from the review of M5 WP-04): a status, an issue type and a choice of an own field are written by their name as shown on screen (status is "In progress", type is Bug), never by a stored key or ID; two names are the same by the one rule that keeps names apart everywhere in the app (bb_core::names::same_name: case and repeated spaces do not count, accents do), so the checker, the choice lists and the server compare alike. The choices of built-in fields (Priority, Status group) are words of the language like the field words: one English word each, defined once next to the choice and the same in every language of the app, never the text of the message catalog. The server turns a name into the things of that name that the person may see, at the moment the search runs; a name the person cannot see is an unknown value, with the same message as a name that does not exist. A rename makes the old name unknown in a saved search, and the checker says so; nothing silently matches something else. A person or a group may be named in a search when the person searching may see that name by Who sees people (ADR-0022, the people kind of the field); member of "…" also needs being in the group or Manage groups, because its results show who is in the group. A project is named by its current short name and an issue by its Issue ID (bb-core), and both only when the person sees them. One function resolves every name of a search, for running it and for checking a saved search (the lead, from the reviews of M5 WP-04 and WP-06). Each word of the language (built-in fields, the words of yes and no, the operators each kind of field allows) is defined once, next to the field, and a word belongs to one field for everyone: an own field never takes the word of a built-in field, also not of one the person may not read or that cannot be searched yet.

  2. Lengths of time are written in hours and minutes (the lead, M5-F41): a field of lengths of time takes 2 hours, 45 minutes or 1 hour 30 minutes, never a number of seconds. The units have one fixed length, minute/minutes and hour/hours only: days and weeks would depend on working hours, and a search text means the same for everyone and in every organization. The printer writes the canonical form in words (1 hour 30 minutes, 90 minutes is 1 hour 30 minutes). A bare number for such a field is a mistake with a plain message that shows how to write it (search.mistake.wrong-duration); a length of time for a field of numbers is a mistake too. The tree holds whole minutes (Operand::Duration) and the server turns them into the seconds the field stores. The search bar writes the same words on the filter button and in its window. A length of time is never a choice: size is 2 hours is a mistake for a field with a list of choices, even when a choice is spelled like it. One function (Operand::spelling) writes the words of a value for the checker, the printer and the store, and TimeUnit carries the minutes of each unit. The words minute(s) and hour(s) are keywords from this decision on: an own field with one of these words is written in quotes by the printer ("hours" is 3), a text that wrote it bare before is still read by the field of that word and printed with quotes (canonical print, M5 WP-07). Repeated or reversed units (30 minutes 1 hour) are accepted and printed in the canonical order. Enforced by: the vectors of the language (cargo xtask gen search-vectors, with timeSpent), TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP.

  3. The words of the glossary, with spaces and in display case (decision D3 of the exit polish of M5): a field is written as the glossary names it, in lower case and with spaces (status group, assigned to, found in release), and the values of the built-in lists in display case (priority is High, status group is not Done; a value of several words is quoted, as every name with spaces is: "In progress"). The name of a field runs up to the word that starts what is asked of it (is, in last, contains, member of, within) or joins or orders (and, or, not, sort, a direction); a name that would be cut by one of these words is written in quotes. As a key of sort by, a name that begins with the words of a direction (highest, z to) is written in quotes too, because after a key those words are its direction (sort by status, "z to"); the parser, the end of a name and the printer share the one rule of where a direction begins (words::starts_direction, found by TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP). One rule tells two words apart (bb_core::fields::word_key: lower case, no space), so the form of the old language (statusGroup, assignedTo, inProgress, any case) still reads, and a saved search stored in it loads. After a text is read with the fields it is for, every field and every value of a fixed list is put in the words the field gives (bb_searchlang::parse_with), so the canonical text, the address, a saved search and the filter buttons show the new words and the round trip between Simple and Advanced search stays lossless (TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP). The word of a built-in field is its key with spaces, of an own field its name as names are told apart (names::name_key); the choices of Priority and Status group are code_phrase of their codes. Hidden fields do not change: only the readable fields are looked at, for the match, the mistake and the suggestions, so no glossary name of a hidden field is given away (QRY-05). Where a text stops before its end (prio is High and ), the mistakes of what stands before the place come first, in reading order. The words of columns and grouping kept in an address or a saved presentation are read by the same rule for the built-in fields. Enforced by: TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP, the tests qry_05_… of bb-searchlang.

Amendment M7: the modules are built for size (M6-F68)

The two modules of the browser were at their budgets: bb_wasm at 153.3 KB with Brotli against 154.0 KB, after the security fix of pulldown-cmark and the sentence of booked time. What a module holds that no browser needs is the formatting of floating point numbers that serde uses in its error texts (about 14 KB before compression) and the Debug texts of panics. Decided:

  1. cargo xtask wasm builds the standard library again for size and lets a panic stop at once (-Zbuild-std=std,panic_abort, -Zbuild-std-features=optimize_for_size, -Cpanic=immediate-abort). A panic of a module then stops it with no text. Measured with Brotli at the server's quality: bb_wasm from 153.3 KB to 133.1 KB, bb-wasm-search from 90.3 KB to 71.5 KB; their budgets in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml come down with them (135.0 KB and 73.0 KB).
  2. Stable means were tried first and measured, and did not get the module under 150 KB. The profile already had opt-level = "z", lto, one codegen unit and panic = "abort"; opt-level = "s" made the module 6 KB bigger, further passes and --converge of wasm-opt changed nothing (153.25 KB to 153.26 KB at best), and giving up the formatted error text of serde_json in the entry points saved 0.65 KB, because serde writes the text of an error when it makes it (the float formatter stays reachable through Unexpected).
  3. The risk is accepted and written down. The three flags are unstable. The stable compiler takes them with RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1, which this one build sets and no other build of the program does. They can break with any update of the toolchain: the toolchain is pinned by rust-toolchain.toml (with rust-src, which the build of the standard library needs), and every update of it must build the modules with cargo xtask wasm and keep the budgets (PERF-BUNDLE) before it is taken in. The follow-up M7-F206 takes the flags out when stable Rust can do the same.

Amendment M8: the modules write no Debug text

The own themes, the dates and the work times took bb_wasm to 166.3 KB with Brotli against its budget of 166.0 KB. A module still held the Debug formatting that nothing in a browser reads: the Debug text of the errors and values it names, and serde quoting a value with {:?} in the text of an error. Decided:

  1. cargo xtask wasm builds the modules with -Zfmt-debug=none: {:?} writes nothing in a module. A refusal of the module is still an error, and the text of a serde error loses only the value it quoted. Measured with Brotli at the server's quality: bb_wasm from 166.3 KB to 163.7 KB; bb-wasm-search stays at 72.1 KB, because it holds no such formatting. The budgets stay as they are.
  2. The flag is unstable, like the three of amendment M7, and is taken in under the same terms: only this build sets it, the pinned toolchain must build the modules with it and keep the budgets before an update is taken in, and M7-F206 takes it out with the others when stable Rust can do the same.

Enforced by

ARCH-PURE, ARCH-WASM, TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0006: Own fields stored in a typed value table

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Organizations add their own fields to issues, time entries, work days, documents, releases and projects. They must be filterable, sortable, permissioned per field, and fast on both databases.

Decision

Store values in one field_value table: (entity_kind, entity_id, field_id, value_text, value_number, value_date, value_ref, position), with indexes per typed column and per (field_id, value_*). Multi-value fields use several rows. Field definitions (type, rules, options, look) live in field and field_option.

Consequences

  • The search compiler joins field_value per referenced field; indexes keep it fast at 1 M issues.
  • Built-in fields stay real columns; own fields and built-in fields look the same to search, permissions and the API.

Alternatives considered

  • A JSON column per entity: indexing differs between SQLite and PostgreSQL and is weaker for sorting. Rejected.
  • Adding real columns at runtime: schema changes from the UI are risky and slow. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-DB-PARITY, PERF-BENCH; table shape: review (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0007: Event log and outbox as the single source of change

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

History, notifications, webhooks, the security log, full-text indexing and live updates all need to know what changed. Writing to each separately would duplicate logic and lose consistency.

Decision

Every use case appends domain events (actor, channel, entity, field changes before → after, reason) in the same transaction as the change, plus an outbox row. After commit, consumers (history, notifications, webhooks, security log, search index, live updates) read the outbox, remember their position, and are idempotent.

Consequences

  • One write path; every consumer sees the same facts.
  • The security log is hash-chained from the security-relevant events.
  • Events contain personal data, so they carry personal-data marks and follow keep-and-delete rules (ADR-0015).

Change (M3 WP-07)

The first consumer of the outbox is the history of an issue (history_entry, ISS-06). It reads events after its stored position and writes one row per event and issue with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so a repeat changes nothing. The rows and the position commit together (M5-F101), so a reader that stops resumes from the position it had, and a repeat (two readers at the same moment, or a restart) is harmless through ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. The rows hold the facts; the reader's field mask is applied when the history is read, never when it is built, so a change of roles changes what is shown at once. The consumer runs when a history is read and as the daily job history.catch-up of the job runner (ADR-0017), which is also queued at every server start (M3-F71).

Alternatives considered

  • Full event sourcing: more power than needed and harder for agents to get right. Rejected; current state stays in normal tables.
  • Database triggers: dialect-specific and invisible in code. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-EVENTS (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0008: API first: OpenAPI from Rust, TypeScript client generated

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

The browser app must be a normal API client (principle 3), and API types must exist once (ODR).

Decision

Describe every endpoint and type in Rust with utoipa; generate the OpenAPI 3.1 document at build time; generate the TypeScript types and a thin fetch client with openapi-typescript into web/packages/api-client. Error codes, permission names and validation schemas are part of the document. The CI check generated-code-freshness fails if the client is out of date.

Consequences

  • The browser can't call what the API doesn't offer; third parties get the same API.
  • API versioning: /api/v1/…; breaking changes need a new version and an ADR.

Amendment M4: the API freeze

Decision M4-Q8, when the API stops changing names:

  • Until m4-done, the only client is Bugaboo's own web app, generated from the same document, so names may still change. M4 WP-02 brings every name in line with the glossary before the freeze.
  • From m4-done on, /api/v1 is frozen. Renaming or removing anything is a breaking change and needs a decision record and a new version:
    • a path, an operation ID, a schema, a property or a parameter;
    • an enum value or an error code.
  • Adding a route, an optional property, an enum value the client must already accept, or an error code stays free.
  • At m4-done the lead stores the generated document as the frozen copy. A check then compares every new document with it and fails on anything removed or renamed (ARCH-API-FREEZE).

Amendment M4 WP-16: the shape the API has at the freeze

The lead decided what the API looks like when it is frozen (the exit review, API changes before the freeze):

  • Every enum value and every error code is written in words joined by hyphens: in-progress, auth.wrong-credentials, workflow.not-named. The message keys follow the same rule, so the key of a code is error. and the code with its dot kept.
  • An issue's ID is readable_id, never key. A path parameter names the thing ({role}, never {role_id}); the groups of labels are label_group, the groups of statuses status_group, and a bare group is people.
  • Dates and times are texts of RFC 3339 (format: date-time), the names of operations say what they do (getDraft, createAssignment, markNotificationsRead), and the enums that are no body have no Body in their names. A change of a field has one shape, change, in the history and in notifications. The thing that is edited is { record: { kind, id }, part } everywhere, with the kind from a closed list.
  • A schema is written once, and a list of fields or workflows is a page like the others. The description writes each shared answer, header and paging parameter once in components.
  • A route that makes something answers 200 with the thing it made, and no Location header: the browser needs the body, and a client finds the thing by its ID. This is the decision of B7; a 201 would be a break after the freeze, so it stays.
  • The capped lists (the previews, the sessions, the use of a field, the level tables) stay capped, with their limits as named constants; a cursor for them is an addition after the freeze.

The frozen copy is tools/checks/api-frozen.json, the generated description in compact form, written by cargo xtask freeze. WP-16 stored the first copy, so ARCH-API-FREEZE already guards the names above; the lead stores the last one at m4-done (and again, with a decision, for a change of a name that must stand before it). ARCH-API-LINT keeps the style: one casing for enum values, no duplicate or orphan schema, no _id in a path parameter. The glossary words in the names of the API are TXT-TERMS, which reads the same description.

Kept in v1 for good (decided by the lead, WP-16)

  • The server status. /api/v1/status, ServerStatus and its routes keep their names. A health route is conventional, and the glossary has a row for server status, so it is not the status of an issue.
  • The paths of previews and of the person. The five patterns of the routes of previews stay. The rule for a new route: /auth is signing in and credentials, /me is one's own preferences.
  • RecordKind is closed. It lists 26 kinds of record, and the use cases refuse those that cannot be edited (the answer is resource.not-found). The enum only grows. A word that is not in it (also the form with an underscore) is refused as an invalid request, 400 request.invalid, in a body and in an address.

Open and closed (decided by the lead, WP-16)

  • Open. Every enum of an answer, every kind union, every oneOf variant and every error code is open: a client must accept a value it does not know, and a new value there is an addition. No answer enum is marked closed today.
  • Closed. What a request names is closed to the server: the values of an enum in a request (RecordKind, a level, a setting type) are refused when unknown, and ARCH-API-FREEZE refuses to take one away or to put a rule on a text that had none.

Kept in v1 for good, schemas (decided by the lead, WP-16)

  • The Page_* names. The 26 schemas that utoipa names Page_X for the page of a list of X keep these names. They are the name of a page of an item, and the client types are made from them.
  • IssueItem. The six operations that answer IssueItem (changeIssue, saveIssueDescription, saveIssueFieldText, moveIssue, restoreIssue, createIssue) keep it: its members are always there when no fields= is sent, so the optional types are only the type of the list.
  • The tables of levels. FieldLevelTableBody, PeopleLevelTableBody and their rows, cells and answers have plain names (a macro writes one struct for each kind of subject), so there is no generic schema name left.

Compatible later (not in the freeze)

These are additions after the freeze and break no client: optional and nullable members that are always there in new bodies (M4-F174), the per-route list of error codes and the wording of the shared 400 and 409 answers (B2), the open fields maps with inline field keys (B11, M4-F177), cursors for the capped lists (M4-F172), a stable cursor in the store for the lists of fields and workflows (M4-F171) and a truncated member of the list of workflows (M4-F180), and an optional version in the body of a change of a person's own setting and the same member in the answer (M5-F97, ADR-0018).

Amendment M6 WP-05: a retired word of a frozen enum

A word of a frozen enum may leave the code when an amendment of the decision that owns it says so: the schema keeps the word marked retired, a request that names it is accepted with no effect, and no answer names it. The first case is activity and cost-center of Field (ADR-0035, amendment WP-05). The frozen copy is not written again.

Amendment M8: the answer of a change of an issue holds the time factor

changeIssue answers IssueAfterChangeBody: every member of IssueItem at the top, as at the freeze (an allOf of IssueItem), and beside them the time factor when the change set the people the issue is assigned to (ADR-0030, amendment M8). The factor is no member of IssueItem, so no list carries it. Adding a member is free under the freeze; the frozen copy is not written again.

Alternatives considered

  • Hand-written TypeScript types: drift. Rejected.
  • GraphQL: flexible, but per-field authorization and query-cost control are harder to make airtight. Rejected; ?fields= gives lean responses.

Enforced by

DOC-GENERATED, ARCH-WEB-API, ARCH-LEAN, ARCH-VERSIONED, ARCH-API-FREEZE (the frozen copy is stored with cargo xtask freeze at m4-done), ARCH-API-LINT (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0009: Browser app: React 19, Vite, TanStack, React Aria

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

The UI must be slick, accessible (WCAG 2.2 AA), fast on phones, and buildable by agents with clear patterns.

Decision

  • React 19 with function components and hooks; Vite for building and splitting.
  • TanStack Router for type-safe routes and typed URL search parameters (searches and presentations live in the URL).
  • TanStack Query as the only store for server data; long lists are drawn with the Virtualizer of React Aria Components (amendment M5).
  • React Aria Components as the base of every interactive component (focus, keyboard, screen readers, touch).
  • Tiptap (ProseMirror) for the document editor; d3-force for the relation map layout; timeline, calendar and charts are our own components on shared primitives.

Consequences

  • No global client state library: URL + query cache + local component state cover the needs.
  • Heavy features are lazy-loaded to meet the 250 KB initial budget, and so are their texts: each feature brings its own part of the message catalog (ADR-0028).

Alternatives considered

  • Next.js / server rendering: adds a Node server to install and complicates the CSP. Rejected.
  • Headless UI kits without accessibility depth: more work to reach WCAG. Rejected.

Amendment M5: one way to draw long lists

Decision M5-Q11: long lists draw only the rows that can be seen with the Virtualizer of React Aria Components, which the people list already uses (M2-F84), not with TanStack Virtual: one library for every long list, and the keyboard and screen-reader behaviour of React Aria come with it. @tanstack/react-virtual is not added.

Enforced by

ARCH-WEB-FEATURES, PERF-BUNDLE, TEST-A11Y, LINT-TS (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0010: Styling through design tokens only

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04 · the styling decisions (the token file, the generator, CSS Modules) are replaced by ADR-0026; the rest stands · amended in M8: themes of your own

Context

Four built-in themes, a theme editor, custom field looks and strict CSP, all without letting customization inject code.

Decision

  • design/tokens.json (W3C Design Tokens format) is the only source of colors, fonts, sizes, radii and shadows, for all four themes. Replaced by ADR-0026: design/theme.kdl is the only source of every value and every component rule.
  • cargo xtask gen tokens produces: CSS variables per theme, TypeScript token names, and the Rust validation used by the theme editor (allowed values, contrast checks). Replaced by ADR-0026: cargo xtask gen theme writes the one style sheet, the TypeScript names and the Rust theme choices.
  • Components use CSS Modules with var(--token) only. The hooks reject raw colors, pixel sizes outside tokens and inline styles. Replaced by ADR-0026: components carry no class names and no styles; they emit data-part, data-variant and data-state, and the rules in the theme file use tokens only.
  • Custom themes and field looks store token values or token names, never CSS.
  • The choices of a person that are not a theme (Compact spacing, Larger text, Less motion) are variants in the token file: each switches token values through an attribute on the page (data-spacing, data-text, data-motion), and Less motion also follows the device. Sizes of spacing and text are written as the usual size times a factor token, so one choice scales everything. Where the layout changes (bp-tablet, bp-computer) is a token too, read by the app through the generated TypeScript.
  • Every theme has stronger colors for prefers-contrast: more (contrastMore). STY-CONTRAST checks them at 7:1 for text and 3:1 for lines.

Amendment (M8, themes of your own)

Own themes (the custom themes of the decision above) still store token values and never CSS. How they are checked, served and limited is decided in ADR-0026, update M8: the allowed values and the contrast checks that this record gave to a generated Rust validation now live in bb-core (the token list written by cargo xtask gen theme, the contrast maths moved from xtask), shared by STY-CONTRAST, the server and the theme editor.

Consequences

  • The design pages in docs/design/ use the generated CSS (theme.css, the tokens without the component rules).

Alternatives considered

  • Tailwind CSS: harder to enforce "tokens only"; class soup in agent-written code. Rejected.
  • CSS-in-JS at runtime: costs performance and needs CSP exceptions. Rejected.

Enforced by

STY-TOKENS, LINT-CSS, STY-CONTRAST (see tools/checks/catalog.toml); for the styling decisions that ADR-0026 replaced, THEME-ONLY too.

ADR-0011: One Markdown renderer for server and browser

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04 · changed (M3 WP-02: the writer replaces ammonia, see "Change")

Context

Issue descriptions, comments and documents are Markdown written by people, so they're untrusted. The preview must match what others will see.

Decision

bb-markdown uses pulldown-cmark to parse and writes the HTML itself from the parser's events, with one allow list: only the tags and attributes of its writer can be in the output, raw HTML in the text is turned into text, links get rel="noopener noreferrer" and open outside, only http, https, mailto and our own pages are links, and images come from our own origin or from a host an admin allows. Issue IDs and mentions come back as tokens (resolved later with permission checks), shown as chips. The same crate runs on the server and, via WebAssembly, in the browser for previews.

Consequences

  • One allow list (SSOT), in the writer; no client-side HTML rendering library.
  • Nothing is parsed back and cleaned, so there is no gap between what the writer meant and what a sanitizer's HTML parser reads (mutation XSS has no place to start).
  • The WebAssembly module stays small: the budget of the module is in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml (architecture §8, PERF-04), and the search language has a module and a budget of its own (ADR-0005, amendment M5).
  • The browser shows the HTML with one Trusted Types policy, bugaboo-markdown, in the one component MarkdownView (SEC-RICHTEXT).
  • The document editor (Tiptap) stores Markdown; its schema is limited to what bb-markdown renders.

Change (M3 WP-02)

The first plan was to sanitize with ammonia after pulldown-cmark's own HTML. Measured on the real module: ammonia brings an HTML parser (html5ever), the URL library with its tables for international domain names, and their data, about 250 KB more with Brotli, so the module would be about four times the size of the parser alone, far over its budget, which the search language (M5) has to share. Writing the HTML from the events needs none of that, is easier to read as one allow list, and keeps the security property: the output holds only what the writer can write. The corpus test (SEC-13) and the property tests check the output for tags, attributes and addresses that the allow list does not have.

Change (M3 WP-07)

A comment is shown to many readers, and what a token may become depends on the reader: an issue ID is a chip only for a reader who may see that issue, a mention only if the writer may name that person. The renderer stays pure and knows nothing of this. Options.plain_tokens lists the places (in Rendered::tokens) that stay plain text; the server renders once to find the tokens, decides, and renders again with the list. The places do not move, so the decision is made on the same list both times. The rendering is per reader and never stored.

Alternatives considered

  • marked/markdown-it + DOMPurify in the browser: a second renderer that could disagree with the server. Rejected.
  • pulldown-cmark + ammonia (the first plan): a clean-up after the HTML is made; too big for WebAssembly (see "Change"). Rejected for the browser module, and one renderer must serve both.

Enforced by

ARCH-PURE, ARCH-WASM, SEC-PATTERNS, SEC-RICHTEXT, PERF-BUNDLE (the budget of the module) (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0012: One binary for sold and served

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Bugaboo may be sold (self-hosted) or served (hosted by us); the business model isn't decided.

Decision

  • The same signed binary runs in both models (DIST-01).
  • Served = one isolated instance per customer (own database, file store, encryption key and address) in the EU, plus a separate control plane for set-up, updates, backups and health (DIST-02). The control plane uses an operator API that cannot read customer data; emergency access needs the customer's approval and is logged in their security log (DIST-03).
  • Sold: a signed offline license file; no phone-home and no telemetry (DIST-04).
  • Export and import work between the two, both ways (DIST-06).

Consequences

  • "One organization per installation" stays true in both models; no tenant column in every table.
  • Hosting cost per customer is higher than a shared multi-tenant system; accepted for isolation and simplicity.

Alternatives considered

  • Multi-tenant shared database: cheaper to host, but every query needs a tenant filter and one bug can leak across customers. Rejected for 1.0.

Enforced by

review (deployment design; tested end to end in the served-model milestone), DEP-LICENSES for the license file tooling (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0013: AI: one provider interface, one tool registry, no decisions about people

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

AI is priority three, but must never bypass permissions, must resist prompt injection, and must stay outside the AI Act's high-risk and banned uses.

Decision

  • One provider trait with adapters for Anthropic (default) and OpenAI-compatible endpoints (covers local models).
  • One tool registry used by both the assistant and MCP. Each tool calls a bb-app use case as the actor.
  • Assistant writes are proposals; nothing changes until the person clicks Apply.
  • Context builder sends only readable, non-excluded fields and fences people's text as untrusted.
  • Designed out: tools that rank, evaluate or assign people, read working hours, or analyse mood. They don't exist in the registry.
  • AI output saved into issues or documents is marked Written with the assistant.

Consequences

  • MCP and the assistant can't drift apart in rules or capabilities.
  • Adding a tool needs a review against the AI Act rules (checklist in the ADR template).

Alternatives considered

  • Separate tool code for MCP and the assistant: duplicates permission handling. Rejected.
  • Letting the assistant act directly: prompt-injection risk. Rejected.

Amendment (M7, where the parts live, the settings and what goes to a provider)

The maintainer accepted every recommendation of M7-Q1 to Q10 on 2026-11-07. What changes here:

  • Where the parts live (architecture §4). Every tool is a bb-app use case run as the actor, the assistant is a bb-app use case, and bb-app imports no adapter (architecture §4, rule 2). So the tool registry and the context builder live in bb-app (crates/bb-app/src/ai/), next to the use cases they call, and do no I/O of their own. bb-ai holds the provider adapters (Anthropic and OpenAI-compatible) behind the port AiProvider of bb-app, and the test fake behind its feature testing; bb-server wires the adapter. bb-mcp turns the registry into MCP with rmcp and depends on bb-app only (ADR-0042). Enforced by: ARCH-DEPS, ARCH-AI-TOOLS (it reads crates/bb-app/src/ai/tools/** and crates/bb-mcp/**).
  • The settings of AI (topic AI of the registry, ADR-0018 amendment M7; Organization settings › Connections › AI, UX §5.1):
    • AI is off for the organization at the start (AI-02, PRIV-08), and each project has a switch that follows the project above until it has its own; AI counts at a place only when the organization and that place have it on (one function, AI counts here, which the assistant, MCP and agents ask);
    • the AI provider (Anthropic or OpenAI-compatible, which covers a Local model), the model, the address (for OpenAI-compatible) and the API key, kept as a stored secret under the master key (architecture §7, Secrets and keys) and never shown again; a change of the provider or the address asks for the administrator's password again, only HTTPS goes to an outside provider, an address on the local network is allowed only for the OpenAI-compatible choice, and Try the provider is the one call that may be made while AI is off: it sends only the fixed try text and no data of the organization, needs the agreement of an outside provider first, and is limited to one try in 10 seconds per person; an error of the provider becomes one sentence ("The AI provider did not answer") and is never shown in its own words (it can repeat what the internal network answered);
    • the agreement step: before an outside provider is switched on, the administrator confirms that a Data processing agreement is in place (PRIV-08); a local model needs none. The confirmation is stored with who gave it, when and for which provider, and is in the security log; changing the provider asks again;
    • What goes where: the page lists what may be sent (the text and the fields the person reads, without Never sent to AI), to which provider and in which country;
    • Send names of people (M7-Q5, off at the start), and whether AI apps may sign in, with the web return addresses an administrator allows (ADR-0042, decision 3). Enforced by: ARCH-SETTINGS, and the tests ai_02_ai_is_off_at_the_start_and_no_call_leaves_the_server and priv_08_an_outside_provider_needs_the_agreement_before_it_is_switched_on (WP-02).
  • Never sent to AI in M7 (AI-03) is a mark on a field and on a project (with its sub-projects): the context builder leaves the field or the project's issues out even for a person who reads them, and a search sent through a tool that names a field kept from AI is refused like an unknown field (QRY-05). Administrators mark fields and any project (Change organization settings); a project lead marks their own project (Change project settings there). Restricted issue groups follow when restricted issues come (SEC-05, 1.0; M7-Q10). It holds for every way AI reaches Bugaboo, because all of them read through the one registry and the one context builder: the assistant, AI apps through MCP and agents. Enforced by: the tests ai_03_a_field_never_sent_to_ai_is_not_in_the_context_even_when_the_person_reads_it, ai_03_a_project_never_sent_to_ai_keeps_its_sub_projects_out_too and ai_03_a_search_through_a_tool_that_names_a_field_kept_from_ai_is_refused_like_an_unknown_field, and TEST-PROMPT-INJECTION.
  • Names of people (M7-Q5). With an outside provider, a person in the context is sent as their role label ("a Team member"), and the asking person as "you", never by name, handle or e-mail address, unless an administrator switched on Send names of people; What goes where says which is in force. A local model gets people as the asking person sees them (Who sees people). MCP is not affected: an AI app acts as the person and reads people as the person reads them (AI-04). Enforced by: the test ai_04_for_an_outside_provider_people_are_named_by_role_and_the_asker_as_you, and SEC-MATRIX.
  • The conversation of the assistant (M7-Q6) lives in the open panel only and is not stored on the server; closing the panel ends it.
  • The log of a tool call (M7-Q6) is one row with who (the person, the actor kind, the app or the agent), which tool, reads or changes, the size in and out, the time and the outcome; never the content of either. It is kept 90 days, then deleted. A refused call also writes a row of the security log. Content logging for troubleshooting is not built in M7 (architecture §7, AI, changes with this). Enforced by: DATA-LOGS.
  • The author marks of untrusted text. The context builder and every tool answer fence each text of a person (a title, a description, a comment, a field value, a file name) as data, with an author mark that says who wrote it: someone in the project, a Guest, someone outside, an agent, the assistant (AI-05, ADR-0029 decision 9). A fence cannot be closed from inside the text. Enforced by: TEST-PROMPT-INJECTION.
  • What the assistant does in M7 (M7-Q2). The panel answers what the person types about what it looks at (the issue, the list, the project), with the read tools, and proposes changes with the write tools; "Summarize the comments on WEB-142" works as a typed question. The buttons of AI-12, AI-13 and AI-14, the catch-up and the suggestions beside the fields stay in M12.
  • Usage limits and cost budgets per person and organization (AI-06) stay in M12 (M7-Q10); M7 has only the limits of agents and keys (ADR-0029, amendment M7).

Amendment (M7, the assistant on the server)

  • A question and its answer. POST /api/v1/assistant/questions carries the text the person typed, what the panel looks at (at most five: an issue, the search of a list, a project) and the turns so far, which the browser keeps and sends back (M7-Q6). The server stores no conversation. The use case reads through the tools of the registry as the person, only as previews, at most the number of tools the settings allow (8 at the start; amendment WP-15) and one round more with the provider for one question; the last round is given no tools. A session asks; an access key, also the key of an AI app, is turned away (AI apps work through MCP).
  • Proposals. A tool that changes something comes back as a proposal: the tool, its input exactly as previewed, the fields with the value now and after, and a reference. The reference is a signature of the person, a moment 10 minutes ahead, a random word and the tool with its input, made under the key of the signed links with a signature domain of its own; the input travels beside it and is bound into the signature, so a changed byte, another tool or another person does not open it. A reference works once: the random word is kept in assistant_reference until the reference runs out, and a second Apply answers ai.proposal-invalid.
  • Apply (POST /api/v1/assistant/apply) checks the reference, then runs the preview of the tool again as the person, now, and the use case of the tool with the same request (one reading of the input for both), through the channel assistant. A version that moved on is refused with the newer value as for a person; an issue kept from AI since is not found. There is no other way to save.
  • Nothing about people is decided. A proposal that changes Assigned to is shown only when the question holds the word assign and the name of every person it puts there, as the person sees that name; otherwise the model is told it was not proposed. Enforced by: comp_10_the_assistant_never_proposes_a_person_by_its_own_choice.
  • The answer is written by the one Markdown writer with the option for AI answers: no picture is ever shown, every link shows its full address, issue IDs and names stay text. Enforced by: ai_05_an_answer_never_loads_an_outside_picture_and_shows_links_in_full, SEC-RICHTEXT.
  • A project with the assistant switched off is kept from the assistant like a project with the mark Never sent to AI: the one read of what is withheld (withheld(kind)) holds it, so every tool the assistant calls and the context builder leave it out, and the assistant answers AI is off for a project the panel names. While the organization has the assistant off, the ways in refuse before they read anything. Since WP-15 this is true of the assistant only: AI apps and agents follow their own switches (amendment WP-15). Enforced by: ai_02_a_project_with_ai_switched_off_is_kept_from_every_tool.

Amendment (M7, WP-15): each kind of AI is its own switch, and the look-ups are a setting

The maintainer's comments of 2026-11-09 on the settings of AI. They change decisions above where they say so.

  • Three kinds, three switches, none depends on another. The assistant is the setting ai.enabled (off at the start), AI apps ai-apps.enabled (on at the start) and agents agents.enabled (on at the start; since M9 both start off in a new installation, the amendments of ADR-0029 and ADR-0042). Each has a value for the organization and may have one for each project (ai-apps.enabled gains the project level; the other two had it). Switching one off, for the organization or for a project, never switches another off. This replaces "AI has to be on for the organization as well" for AI apps (ADR-0042) and "a project with AI off is kept from every way in" (above).
  • One rule for the project chain. For a kind, the nearest value along the chain of a project decides (its own, else its parent's, up to the organization's); a sub-project that is switched on again is on below a parent that is off. The rule is written once (Ctx::projects_with_kind_off, bb-app/src/ai/kinds.rs) and used by the withheld read of every caller and by the narrowing of agents. withheld(kind) holds the marks (Never sent to AI keeps all three out) and the projects where that kind is off, for the caller that asks: ToolCaller is the kind.
  • The doors. The door of OAuth (registration, the swap of a code, a token) and of an access key at /mcp follows ai-apps.enabled only; an agent key follows agents.enabled only (the narrowing of the agent); the assistant follows ai.enabled only, and has no way in at /mcp. When both AI apps and agents are off, /mcp reads nothing at all, so a refusal is no guess of a network.
  • What the project settings show. The card Agents, AI apps and the assistant shows the three switches in the order agents, AI apps, the assistant last, each named for its kind (Agents in this project, AI apps in this project, Assistant in this project), then Never sent to AI. Each of the first two offers As the organization (on|off) or As WEB (on|off), On where the level above is off, and Off; the assistant keeps its switch and Follow the organization again. The card says that each can be switched by itself and that the mark holds for all three. No stored data changes, so there is no migration.
  • The look-ups of the assistant (decision "At most 8 tools" above becomes a setting). assistant.look-ups-most (organization, administrators; 2, 4, 8, 12, 20, 50 or No limit; 8 at the start) is the most tools one question may run. assistant.look-ups (each person, My settings › Assistant; As the organization or a number) is a lower number for one's own questions. The number that counts is the lower of the two, read when the question is asked, so a person never goes above the most of the organization even when the organization lowers it later. No limit is no limit: nothing stops the look-ups of a question (the maintainer's decision, 2026-11-09), so it can cost more; the time limit of each call to the provider (60 seconds) still holds. For the same reason the question to the assistant (POST /api/v1/assistant/questions) has no fixed time limit of the request (TIME_LIMIT, 30 seconds, still holds for every other route of /api): it ends with the answer, or when the client disconnects (the person closes the panel or the connection drops), which drops the question and so stops the loop with the provider. Enforced by: the tests m7_wp15_every_api_request_has_a_time_limit_but_the_question_to_the_assistant and m7_wp15_a_question_whose_person_has_gone_asks_the_provider_no_more. The help texts write no bounds (TXT-CATALOG). Enforced by: the tests m7_wp15_* in bb-app (ai_switches, assistant_look_ups), bb-core and the server tests on both databases.
  • Order. Everywhere the three are named together (the guide, the settings pages, the user documentation) the order is agents, AI apps, the assistant last.

Enforced by

ARCH-AI-TOOLS, ARCH-PERMS, ARCH-DEPS, ARCH-SETTINGS, SEC-MATRIX, DATA-LOGS, TEST-PROMPT-INJECTION (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0014: One check runner for hooks, agents and CI

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Checks (formatting, linting, hard-coded text, tokens only, terminology, licenses, register, architecture docs, personal-data marks, size budgets) must behave the same on Windows, Linux and WSL, for people, AI agents and CI.

Decision

  • cargo xtask is the single entry point: cargo xtask check staged, check all, gen …, release …. It's Rust, so it runs wherever the code builds.
  • lefthook runs check staged on commit, check push on push and the commit-message check; cargo xtask setup installs it and the hooks.
  • Claude Code hooks (.claude/settings.json) run the relevant checks after each file edit, so agents get immediate feedback.
  • The full local run (cargo xtask ci) runs check all plus slow checks (benchmarks, end-to-end, SBOM). There is no hosted CI (ADR-0037).
  • Rust: rustfmt formats, clippy lints (warnings are errors, selected pedantic lints on).
  • TypeScript 7: oxfmt formats; oxlint lints, with oxlint-tsgolint for type-aware rules. tsgolint is built on typescript-go, the TypeScript 7 compiler itself, so it understands TypeScript 7 exactly. tsc (TypeScript 7) does the type check.
  • CSS: stylelint enforces "tokens only"; formatting by oxfmt (or Biome, if oxfmt doesn't cover CSS at setup time).
  • Other files: taplo (TOML), rumdl (Markdown), typos (spelling), lychee (links).
  • Pattern rules across Rust and TypeScript (no literal UI text, no raw colors, no unwrap in production code, no SQL built with format!, Authorized<T> only in bb-policy) are ast-grep rules in tools/rules/.
  • Every check is listed once in tools/checks/catalog.toml (ADR-0020).

Consequences

  • One list of checks (SSOT), visible in xtask/src/checks/.

Alternatives considered

  • Shell scripts: differ between Windows and Linux. Rejected.
  • ESLint + typescript-eslint: typescript-eslint supports TypeScript only up to 6.0. Rejected.
  • Biome: a good all-in-one tool, but its type-aware rules use its own inference instead of the TypeScript 7 compiler. Kept as fallback for formatting.

Enforced by

META-WIRING, META-CATALOG, META-SPEED, FMT-, LINT- (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0015: Personal-data marks drive GDPR features

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

GDPR features (export, removal, keep-and-delete rules, record of processing) break silently when a new feature adds personal data and forgets them.

Decision

Every stored field is marked in its entity definition with a derive attribute, for example #[personal(category = "employee_time", basis = "legal_obligation")] or #[not_personal]. Unmarked fields fail the build. A generated personal-data map drives Download my data, the Remove a person plan, keep-and-delete jobs, the record of processing (Art. 30) and the data-flow map.

Consequences

  • GDPR compliance becomes part of the type system and CI, not a checklist.
  • Events and logs follow the same marks.

Amendment M6 WP-05: marks by the kind of record

A table that holds rows about many kinds of record (the domain events, the history) marks a field once for every row, and may also mark it for the rows of one kind: #[personal_for(kind = "time_entry", category = "employee_time", basis = "contract")], once for each kind, beside the field's own mark. In those rows the data is about the person of that record (the person of a time entry, of a work day), not the actor of the row. #[derive(Entity)] writes the marks into FieldMark::by_kind (a kind is a word of RecordKind, checked when the program is built), and the personal-data page lists each one under its field. A field marked #[not_personal] for every row, such as the moment of an event, may still be marked for one kind: the moment of an event of a timer or a time entry is when a person started or stopped work. A kind is marked once on a field; the same kind given twice does not build. The working hours of WP-06 mark the reason, the changes and the moment of the events of a work day the same way. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS (the build of the marks), DOC-GENERATED (the page).

Amendment M9 WP-03: the links of a person

The marks say whether a field is personal; the links say whose data a row is (ADR-0044, decision 1). Each field that can name a person says, beside its mark, in which rows it does and what the person is to the row, with a word of Link (author, recipient, subject, actor, holder):

  • a field whose type holds the ID of a person (the types of names_a_person! in bb_core::personal: UserId and Actor, inside Option, Vec, Box, BTreeSet or BTreeMap) carries #[person(author)];
  • a reference to a record (the types of refers_to_a_record!: EntityRef, EntityId) carries #[person_for(record, link = "subject")] when it names a person through the record it refers to, as bb_core::whose::whose says for each kind of record (the record is the person, belongs to a person whose ID is in a field of the record's entity, or is nobody's; a match without a catch-all, so a new kind has to say); kind = "…" names the field that holds the kind when the reference holds only the ID;
  • a reference that holds a person in the rows of an own field of type Person or People carries #[person_for(field_type = "person", key = "field", link = "subject")], once for each type;
  • the text of an e-mail address carries #[person_email(recipient)] (the invitations);
  • the changes of a record (the types of carries_changes!: FieldChange) carry #[person_in_changes]; the walk finds a person in them by the text of their ID wherever it is, and what the person is to the event comes from one place, bb_core::whose::IN_CHANGES, which declares the members that hold a person for each kind of record beside their names (bb_core::whose::members); the in-memory store of the use-case tests stops a test whose event or notification holds a person in a member that is not declared;
  • JSON (the types of holds_json!: serde_json::Value) carries #[person_in_json(subject)], and the walk finds a person in it by the text of their ID (the value of a proposal of an agent, the action of a change to many issues, the payload of a job);
  • a reference or JSON that never names a person carries #[names_no_person].

#[derive(Entity)] writes the links into the entity's marks (EntityMarks::person_links, a PersonLinks), the list that the walk of a person's data reads, and the personal-data page names them under each entity. A link that does not fit the type of its field, an unknown word or field type, a link given twice, two ways on one field, and #[person_for] without link do not build. A field of a type that can name a person (a person, a reference to a record, changes or JSON, also through an alias or a newtype in bb-core) and has no link, and a person inside a type no link sees through, fail DATA-MARKS, which reads the lists of types from the same source. A linked field is stored in one column, or in a kind and an ID in that order. The fields the walk reads from another table (the person a record belongs to, the type of an own field, the address of a person) are named once, in bb_core::whose, and a link the walk cannot turn into a condition is an error, not a miss. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS (the build and the check), DOC-GENERATED (the page), the tests priv_02_every_field_that_names_a_person_has_a_link_on_a_stored_column and priv_02_every_kind_of_record_says_whose_it_is_through_a_stored_owner of bb-store, and the store of the bb-app tests (the members of the changes).

Alternatives considered

  • A hand-maintained spreadsheet of personal data: drifts. Rejected.

Enforced by

DATA-MARKS, DATA-LOGS (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

Amendment (M1)

  • A person's ID is itself personal data: a pseudonym, marked #[personal(category = "identity", basis = "legitimate_interests")]. After Remove a person it is kept only as the link to the Former user … tombstone.
  • #[not_personal] is accepted only for field types that cannot hold personal data (they implement NotPersonal: numbers, moments, IDs of records, the words of the marks, and types that say so). Free text is never on that list. Remaining limits are written on the generated page docs/privacy/personal-data.md.
  • Checked by DATA-MARKS and by the compile-fail tests in crates/bb-core/tests/compile_fail.rs (not_personal_person, not_personal_text).

ADR-0016: Full-text search inside the database

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Text search must respect permissions and work on both databases at the scale target.

Decision

Use SQLite FTS5 and PostgreSQL text search (tsvector with GIN index) behind one port. The search compiler adds the text condition to the same SQL query as the permission predicates. Index updates come from the outbox.

Consequences

  • No second index to secure, back up or rebuild separately.
  • Ranking quality is good, not perfect; acceptable for 1.0.

Alternatives considered

  • tantivy or an external search server: better ranking, but permission filtering outside SQL and another store to protect. Rejected for 1.0.

Amendment M5: words, what is indexed, the order of results

The M5 proposals (M5-Q5, Q6) were accepted. Decided:

  1. No stemming, the same on both databases. Texts are made comparable once, in Rust: lower case, Unicode NFC, split into words by one rule (bb-core). No letter is changed into another (requirement: the text handling is UTF-8 clean): an accent stays and ß stays ß, so müller finds Müller, written as one character or as two, and Muller and Mueller do not. The databases only store and match the words Rust prepared, and both find the same issues: the FTS5 table has the tokenizer ascii, which cuts only at the spaces between the stored words (a prepared word holds nothing but letters, numbers and marks, and the tokenizer changes nothing outside ASCII; unicode61 was tried and folds ς into σ and a combining iota into ι, and drops letters such as ⓐ, so it is not used), and the tsvector of PostgreSQL is made from the stored words split at spaces and matched with quoted lexemes, so no parser of the locale decides what a word is. German and English text behave alike. A word ending in * matches every word that starts with it; at least two letters stand before the * (a search limit, architecture §7).

    A word has at most 255 bytes (MAX_WORD_BYTES in bb-core). A real word is never that long, and a longer run (a line of Chinese text without a stop, a hash) is not what anybody searches for; PostgreSQL refuses a word of 2047 bytes or more, and one such word in a comment would stop the whole text from being stored. So a longer run is left out when a text is stored (the other words of the text stay, and the text is stored), and a longer word typed in a search is refused by the checker with a message (the same checker in the browser and on the server; it counts the lower-cased word as typed, in bytes). One edge: NFC can make a word that passed the checker longer (a letter that takes apart into more bytes; the most is a few times as long, far below the limit of PostgreSQL, a test proves it). Such a word is looked up as it is, and because the index never keeps a word that long it is found nowhere; an issue must have every word of a search, so that search finds nothing. The port does the same for a caller that did not run the checker, and no word of that length reaches a database.

    Two steps, each with one rule. The checker of the search language decides on the text as typed (lower case, split, no NFC): how many words a contains has and how many letters stand before a *, so the browser and the server answer alike. The words that are stored and looked up come from the whole text put into NFC first and then split. The NFC step is behind the feature canonical-text of bb-core, which the store switches on, because its tables are too large for the search module of the browser, which never prepares a word for the index. A start that NFC shortens below two letters (a syllable written as two jamo and typed with *) passes the checker and is looked up as the whole word.

  2. What is indexed: the title, the description, each comment, the names of attached files, and the own long-text fields. Each text is a row of its own with its source (title, description, a comment, a file, a field), so the search can leave out every source the reader may not see: a field they may not read, a comment or a file on an issue they do not see. A hit never comes from a hidden text.

  3. contains on its own searches the title, the description, the comments and the names of attached files (M5-Q6); <field> contains "…" searches one long-text field, only if the reader may read it. What is inside a file is not searched.

  4. All the words of a contains must be found in the issue, each in any of the texts searched (the lead, from the review of M5 WP-05): contains "login error" finds an issue with login in its title and error in a comment. One contains holds a limited number of words (a search limit, architecture §7), so the statement stays bounded.

  5. The order of results when a search has text and no sort by: issues whose title has the words first, then the newest, then the Issue ID. The words that decide it are those of the first contains on its own that every found issue must meet (not one inside or or not); a search without such a contains is ordered newest first (the lead, from the review of M5 WP-04).

  6. The index is a reader of the outbox (ADR-0007): it keeps its place, catches up after a restart, and bugaboo search-index rebuild can make it again from the stored texts. When the rule that prepares a text changes, a migration empties the index and puts a mark on the place of the reader (migration 25, REBUILD_WANTED). The server then, beside the jobs, takes the head of the outbox, makes the rows of every issue again a page and a transaction at a time, and puts the reader at that head. Until it has finished, the index is empty or partial and a search finds less; the jobs do not wait, and the reader reads no event until the rebuild is done, then reads what came after the head. The start of the server, bugaboo search-index rebuild and the program that makes the large sample organization all use that one store function (take the head, make the rows page by page, move the reader to the head, only forward, so a reader that has gone past the head by itself stays where it is). Like the other commands that look after an installation, the command migrates nothing: it stops with a sentence when the data is older than the program, because an index made under the old rule would be emptied again by the migration at the next start. A benchmark dataset carries a marker with the number of the migration that last changed the rule (RULE_MIGRATION): the program that makes the dataset builds its index and writes the marker, and cargo xtask bench builds the index again with the command when the marker is older or missing.

    Two servers on one database both rebuild when both start while the mark is set. That is correct and only costs the work twice: each page is one transaction under the advisory lock of the index, the rows of an issue are replaced by what the stored texts say at that moment, so the second pass writes the same rows or newer ones; both take the head before they read, and the reader only moves forward. A lock for the whole rebuild is not taken, because it would hold a connection for as long as the data is large. If the rebuild fails the worker tries again after a wait that doubles up to a minute, and a rebuild task that panics is logged and started again.

Enforced by: ARCH-DB-PARITY (the same issues in the same order on both databases), SEC-MATRIX (the search entry point with a hidden field, comment and file), and the tests of M5 WP-05.

Enforced by

SEC-MATRIX (search entry point), ARCH-DB-PARITY (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0017: Background jobs stored in the database

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Previews, virus scans, e-mail, webhooks, digests, backups, keep-and-delete runs and person removal need reliable background work.

Decision

A small job queue in the database (job table with run_at, attempts, lease) run by bb-jobs inside the server process. Leases use SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on PostgreSQL and the single writer queue on SQLite. The jobs that come back every day repeat every 24 hours, fixed in the code (bb_app::jobs::DAILY); a schedule that people set (cron-like) becomes a setting in the registry when a job needs one (M9).

Consequences

  • Nothing extra to install; jobs survive restarts.
  • Throughput is enough for the scale target; heavy work (previews) is limited by a worker pool size setting.

Alternatives considered

  • Redis/RabbitMQ: more installation and attack surface. Rejected.

Enforced by

review; every job type has an idempotency test (part of ARCH-EVENTS test harness) (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

Amendment (M3 WP-08)

  • The runner exists (bb-jobs). It depends on bb-app only (ARCH-DEPS): spawn(services, every) calls Ctx::run_due_jobs() on a timer, and bb-server starts it. The queue is behind the port JobStore; a round takes up to five due jobs under a lease of 120 seconds, runs each, reports it done (it leaves the queue) or failed, and a job that did a step queues the next one when more is left. A job that failed five starts goes to the dead-letter list.
  • Kinds so far: many-changes.step (changing many issues: 100 issues in a step, progress kept in the table change_run after each issue, so a step that stops half way goes on at the next issue and no issue is changed twice) and issues.renew-ids (ADR-0021). many-changes.step judges again at run time what it does to each issue, with the permissions of the person who asked (Ctx::acting, ctx_acting_as). issues.renew-ids judges nothing: it finishes a change that was judged when the person changed the mode of IDs (they needed the right to change the project's settings then), so it renews the IDs of every issue of the project that does not have the new mode yet, and names that person on the events. Both are idempotent.
  • When a change is a job: more than 1,000 issues (MANY_CHANGES_JOB_ABOVE); an access key may not start one (auth.access-key-not-allowed, M3-F121).
  • Jobs that come back every day. editing.purge-drafts (drafts, notes for people who were editing and lock rows that ran out) and history.catch-up (the history reads the events, ADR-0007) are daily kinds; there is no timer of the server any more (M3-F30, M3-F71). bb-server calls Ctx::start_daily_jobs when it starts, which queues a round of each at once, and every round queues the next one a day later before it does its work, so a round that fails (the queue tries it again) or a worker that stops does not end the days. A round queues the next only when none for a later time waits (JobStore::later_job_waits), so a server that starts twice in a day leaves one chain of rounds, not two. Both are idempotent, and a read of a history still catches up first. The index of the text search (ADR-0016) and the notifications have no daily kind: every round of the jobs (run_due_jobs) catches them up, the first round after a start included.
  • Permissions are cached for one step. A step of many-changes.step judges its (up to 100) issues with one context, which keeps what the policy engine decided for the person for the whole step (ADR-0025, decision 3: the cache lives as long as its context). A person who loses access while a run goes on is therefore stopped at the next step, not at the next issue: the next step builds a new context and judges from the roles they hold then, and the issues it leaves alone are named with not-found or not-allowed.
  • A stopped worker and the count. The change to an issue and the saving of the progress of the run are two writes. The event of every change a run makes carries a reason that names the run and the item (ManyChangeRun::item_reason); a step that begins at an item whose event is there already (ManyChangeStore::event_with_reason, looked up by the range of event IDs since the run began) counts the issue as changed and goes on, instead of judging it again and reporting that it changed after the preview.
  • A tag or label counts the version. Putting a tag or a label on an issue or taking one off counts the version of the issue up in the same change (by one, whatever the version stored then is: the routes do not take a version, so two people who add or take off different ones both succeed, and so does a tag put on while somebody saves the title; the event carries the version the row has after the count-up. The other way round, a save that read the version before the tag was put on is told that the version changed, like after any other change. An issue that went to the trash in between is not found), so a preview that read the version before sees that the issue changed in between and names it, also in a Pick one group where the label it would replace is not the one the issue has now.
  • One project event for the renewal. ChangeStore::record_changes writes a change with any number of events of its own, also none. A step of issues.renew-ids writes the events of the issues it renews; the step that renews the last also writes the one event of the project (issue-ids).

Amendment (M4 WP-05)

  • Kinds of files. files.preview makes the preview of one attachment (the payload names the attachment, not the file): every attachment has a job of its own, also one of a file that is stored already, which takes an existing preview of the same content only when it runs. It is not daily. files.clean-up is a daily job: unfinished uploads a day after their last part, attachments after their 30 days in the trash, and files that nothing points to. Both are idempotent, and a preview job that failed for good ends the attachment (and the file, while nobody made a preview) as without a preview.

Amendment (M5, nightly speed runs)

  • Statistics of the database. statistics.refresh is a daily job, queued at every start like the others: on SQLite it runs SQLite's own ANALYZE of each table that SQLite reports out of date (it has rows and no statistics yet, or grew or shrank tenfold), one table at a time, and writes an empty table down as empty; otherwise it does nothing. PostgreSQL keeps its own statistics, and the job does nothing there. It writes no event: it changes no data. Idempotent: a second round finds nothing out of date (adr_0017_the_statistics_job_writes_no_event_and_its_next_round_does_nothing, both databases).

Amendment (M6, time and working hours)

  • Kinds of M6 (ADR-0035):
    • No job deletes working hours: after the keep period an administrator deletes them (ADR-0035, decision 7). The daily kind working-hours.delete-old of the first plan was dropped by the maintainer's decision, and no job counts the old days either: the settings page counts them when it is read.
    • timers.long-running is not daily: it is queued once for each timer, when the timer starts, for its start plus the longest day of the working-time rules (ADR-0035, decision 3). It marks the timer and queues the one notification; a timer that was stopped, switched or thrown away before then leaves it nothing to do, and a timer that was already marked is not told twice. A Change start time queues the job of the new start; the job of the old start finds a start that differs from its payload and does nothing.
  • The statistics keep away from the start (M5-F168). statistics.refresh is not in the round that Ctx::start_daily_jobs queues at a start: its round of a start is queued QUIET_KIND_AFTER_START (5 minutes) later, and every round after that at QUIET_HOUR (03:00) of the time zone the organization chose under Region (UTC when it chose none). The one schedule of the daily jobs is the rhythm of each kind (JobKind::rhythm in bb_app::jobs): FromTheStart (at every start, then every DAILY) for every other kind, QuietHour for the statistics; a match without a catch-all, so a new kind has to say. A round queues the next only when none for a later time waits, as before, so a start within the day leaves one chain (adr_0017_the_start_round_queues_no_statistics_refresh).
  • A write that meets the upkeep is tried again. While Database::refresh_statistics runs it marks the upkeep (db/upkeep.rs in bb-store). A write that meets SQLite's busy answer meanwhile, after the busy timeout every writer has (SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT, unchanged), is tried again, BUSY_WRITE_TRIES times in all with BUSY_WRITE_WAIT between.
