They have field permissions with the starting levels of Estimated time, a search word each (start date, due date) with the comparisons the search language has for dates, a place on forms and in layouts, and a column in lists. Due date is no longer blocked on forms (M3-F101). A Start date after the Due date of the same issue is refused with a sentence that names both. Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX (the field levels of both fields), TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP, ARCH-DB-PARITY, ARCH-API-FREEZE (two optional members, nothing renamed).
  2. A timeline may use other date fields. The timeline is a view of a saved search (ADR-0034, the kind ViewKind::Timeline). It uses Start date and Due date unless the view names two own date fields instead, chosen in the view and stored with it. Dragging a bar changes the fields the view uses, each under its field permissions. A field the reader cannot read counts as empty for that reader, so the issue waits in Not scheduled yet and nothing tells that the field exists (UX §1, Hidden stays hidden). Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX (the timeline route under field levels), the tests of WP-06.
  3. How a bar gets its days. A bar covers whole days, from its first day to its last day, both included.
    • With both dates, the bar runs from the start date to the due date.
    • With Plan by effort on (ADR-0030, decision 3), an issue with Estimated time and a person on the bar gets its other date worked out when it has only one: forward from the start date, or back from the due date. With both dates the bar keeps them, and Not enough days says when the effort does not fit; the due date never moves.
    • Otherwise an issue with one date is a bar of one day on that date.
    • An issue with no date waits in Not scheduled yet. Worked-out days are shown, never stored: a date is stored only when a person or a tool sets it. Enforced by: the tests of WP-06 (plan_12_…), review (a reviewer sees in the plan's code that only a change of an issue writes a date).
  4. The date effect of a kind of relation (M8-Q2). A kind of relation gets a date effect: none, or Must finish first. In M8 Must finish first is the only effect. The starting kind blocks has it: the issue that blocks must finish first, and the one it blocks waits. An organization may give it to one other kind as well, so at most two kinds carry it; whoever may change kinds of relation (Manage issue types, kinds of relation and layouts for the whole organization) gives or takes it. The effects start together, finish together and finish when it starts come in V1 (PLAN-02). Enforced by: the tests of WP-03 (plan_02_…), SEC-MATRIX (the route that changes a kind of relation).
    • A relation of a kind with a date effect is a dependency. The timeline draws it as an arrow from the issue that must finish first to the one that waits. The issue page, the relation map and the timeline read the same rows of relations (PLAN-02; architecture §7, Relations): there is no second record of dependencies. Enforced by: review (a second table or type of dependencies is an ODR finding of coding-standards §1).
    • A dependency that would close a loop (A waits for B, and B for A, over any number of steps) is refused when the relation is made, and giving the effect to a kind is refused when its relations hold such a loop; the sentence names one loop. Loops of blocks that are stored already when migration 49 gives it the effect stay, and the timeline draws their arrows without checking an order along them. Enforced by: the tests of WP-03.
  5. A move that breaks a dependency is a warning, never a push. When an issue that waits starts on or before the last day of an issue it waits for, on the days the plan shows, both bars and the list of warnings show the plan warning Delay (ADR-0030, decision 5): "WEB-280 now ends 2 days after WEB-284 starts, and WEB-284 waits for it". Nothing else moves. Its ways out are those of ADR-0030: Move it after moves the issue that waits, and the issues that wait for it in turn, so that each starts on the first day after the one before it ends; a preview names every issue and its new dates before anything is saved. Keep and accept leaves the plan as it is. Plan by effort never moves a start along a dependency by itself. Enforced by: the tests of WP-06 (plan_13_…), review against ADR-0030 (Moving bars by themselves was rejected).
  6. Every change of a date is a change of the issue. A change of Start date or Due date (on a form, by a drag, by Set dates…, by Move it after, by an AI app or an agent) is one event with the old and the new value (ADR-0007). The history shows it ("Lea moved WEB-280 from 3–7 Nov to 10–14 Nov") and Undo takes it back. Move it after with the issues after it is one run, so Undo takes every date of it back in one step. A save carries the version it read: a change made by somebody else in between gets Keep Ben's / Use mine. Enforced by: ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-VERSIONED, TEST-CONCURRENT (two people move the same bar at once).
  7. Goals on the timeline; no releases yet (M8-Q3). A goal with a Due date is drawn as a diamond on that date: it is the milestone of the timeline that PLAN-04 names. A goal's span is a bracket over its sub-issues (UX §4.7). When a sub-issue ends after the due date of its goal, the goal shows Delay with the same ways out: "Lea's away week moves Login screen past the due date of Mobile app 2.0". Releases (ISS-08) join the timeline in M10, and with them rows by release. Enforced by: the tests of WP-06 and WP-09.

Consequences

  • Migration 49 adds the two dates to the issue and the date effect to the kinds of relation, and gives blocks the effect Must finish first. Enforced by: DATA-MIGRATIONS, ARCH-DB-PARITY.
  • Search, forms, layouts, lists and the API know the two fields; the API grows only by additions (ARCH-API-FREEZE).
  • The plan of ADR-0030 reads its dates and dependencies from here, and the timeline draws them. The Delay sentence of ADR-0030, decision 5, changes: nothing "moves too" (ADR-0030, amendment M8).
  • An organization that plans with its own date fields keeps them; it chooses them in the timeline view.

Alternatives considered

  • Only own date fields, chosen in each view: no search word and no starting field permissions, and every organization would first have to set them up. Not taken as the only way; a view may still choose them.
  • Dependencies as a record of their own beside relations: two models for one connection, which PLAN-02 rules out. Rejected.
  • Push the issues that wait when an earlier one moves: what other tools do. It moves dates that people promised, without a person choosing it. Rejected, as in ADR-0030.
  • All four date effects now: the other three are V1 in PLAN-02 and need their own warnings. Not taken.
  • Releases on the timeline in M8: releases are their own record with their own rules (ISS-08, M10). Not taken; a goal's due date stands in for them.

Enforced by

SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-VERSIONED, ARCH-DB-PARITY, ARCH-API-FREEZE, TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP, TEST-CONCURRENT, TEST-A11Y (every drag has a typed alternative: Set dates…, Add dependency…), the tests that WP-03, WP-06 and WP-09 of M8 name, and review against ADR-0030 (no bar moves by itself).

ADR-0044: Download my data and Remove a person

Status: Accepted · 2026-11-18 · refines PRIV-03, PRIV-04, PRIV-06 and ADR-0015, ADR-0022, ADR-0035 decision 7; the answers to M9-Q3 to M9-Q8 and M9-Q11 of the M9 plan

Context

The GDPR gives every person the right to a copy of what an organization stores about them, with the information of Art. 15(1) (purposes, legal basis, recipients, how long it is kept), the right to take it elsewhere (Art. 20) and, within limits, the right to have it erased (Art. 17). Bugaboo promised both from the start: every stored field carries a personal-data mark (ADR-0015), and the marks were meant to drive Download my data and the Remove a person plan. Neither exists yet. Eight milestones of follow-ups wait for them: the events about a person's settings (M2-F75), locks, drafts and notes (M3-F34), file bytes (M4-F52), notifications (M4-F64), the full-text index (M5-F52), private and shared saved searches (M5-F62, M5-F63), agents (M7-F36), the mark of text written with the assistant in exports (M7-F65), work times (M8-F30) and the choice of a theme (M8-F74).

The marks say whether a field is personal and on which legal basis. They do not say whose data a row is. A comment has an author; a notification has a recipient; an away time has its person; an event has an actor and, for a change of a setting, the person whose setting it was. Export and removal both need that answer, and they must not each write it.

The tombstone exists in part already: bb-policy (people.rs) has PersonRef::Former, Target.removed with FormerUser.label, and former_user_label, which draws the random code (tested by priv_13_former_user_labels_are_random_and_unique); resolve already keeps the name of a removed person for the work days (ADR-0035, decision 7). Nothing removes a person yet.

Some records must outlive the person's account: work days, for the keep period, with the person's name for those who may see working hours (ADR-0035, decision 7), and the security log, whose chain cannot be changed. People also leave an organization long before anybody wants their data erased: their account has to stop working at once, while the records stay.

Decision

  1. One walk of a person's data, written once. Every entity that holds a reference to a person says, next to its marks, which of its columns name a person and what that person is to the row (author, recipient, subject, actor, holder). bb-core holds the list (personal::PersonLinks, generated from the entity definitions like the marks), and bb-store answers it with one walk (PersonData port): for one person, every row of every entity that names them, by kind of link. Download my data, Remove a person and the count shown before a removal read this walk and nothing else. A new entity with a person column and no link fails the build. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS (an entity with a person column needs a link), review (the walk is the one place a person's rows are found; a second search for them in the export or the removal is a finding).

  2. Download my data is a file of two halves. A person asks for it in My settings › My data; a job (privacy.export) writes one ZIP file into exports/ in the data folder, and the person gets a notification with a signed link (5 minutes, ADR-0032) while the file is there. The file holds readable pages (plain HTML with the theme's colours in one style sheet of the file, no script, text rendered by bb-markdown) and the same data as JSON, one file per kind of record, with a README that names each field in plain words and gives, for each kind, the information of Art. 15(1): the purpose, the legal basis, how long it is kept and who receives it. Each kind of record and each of its columns is named in the message catalog (personal-kind.<kind>, personal-field.<kind>.<field>), so the headers of the pages and the lines of the README read in plain words and not as names from the code; #[derive(Entity)] takes both keys for every entity that names a person, so a kind or a field without its message does not compile. That information is generated from the marks, the keep list (ADR-0045) and the outside services that are switched on (mail server, AI provider), never written by hand. Text written with the assistant keeps its mark in both halves (COMP-09, M7-F65). The file is kept 7 days, then deleted by the keep rule Data exports (ADR-0045). Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX (the routes of exports for every starting role), DATA-LOGS (the job logs IDs only), DATA-MARKS (every mark carries what the README needs), review (the JSON names follow the glossary).

  3. What is in it (M9-Q7): every row the walk finds as the person's own (their profile, settings, sessions and sign-in history, passkeys without their keys, access keys without their secrets, the issues they reported, the comments and texts they wrote with every version, their time entries, work days with breaks and the reasons of changes, work times and away times with their notes, notifications, follows, mentions of them, saved searches, agents and agent work they are responsible for, the security-log entries that name them, and the files they uploaded, bytes included). Other people appear only as the person may see them at that moment (PersonRef, ADR-0022): the export never shows more than the screens would. Texts of others are not copied, only named where the person is mentioned. The full-text index is left out: it is a copy of texts already in the export (M5-F52). Enforced by: ARCH-PERSON-REF, SEC-MATRIX, review (a reviewer compares the walk's kinds with the list).

  4. An administrator can make the same file for somebody else (M9-Q8): with the new permission Download someone's data (organization, Manage; Administrator at the start; no access key or agent holds it), and always with a reason. It holds what the person's own export holds, whatever else the administrator may read, because it answers that person's request. The person is told by e-mail at the address on record (also when they are switched off and cannot read a notification) and in the app; the security log records who made it for whom and why. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-EVENTS.

  5. Switch off before Remove (M9-Q4). Switch off (with Manage people) ends a person's sign-in at once: sessions, access keys, OAuth grants of AI apps and the person's agents stop (M7-F36), invitations they made are taken back. Their standing rules end; their open assignments and project memberships stay, with the person marked switched off in pickers, until somebody changes them, because who takes the work over is a person's decision (M9-Q5; COMP-10). Switch on gives the sign-in back. A switched-off person counts as nobody for notifications, picks and limits, and keeps every record. Each switch-off is written to the replay list (decision 8). Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX (a switched-off person's session, key and agent are refused), ARCH-PERMS.

  6. Remove a person is final and has one plan. With the new permission Remove people (organization, Manage; Administrator at the start; no key or agent), after a window that says what is deleted now, what stays with Former user K7Q2 and what is kept by law until when, all read from the walk and the keep rules (ADR-0045). Only a switched-off person is removed. One change then:

    • deletes the account and everything that only serves it: password, passkeys, two-step data, sessions, access keys, grants, handle, settings and the choice of theme (M8-F74), private saved searches (M5-F62), drafts, locks and notes (M3-F34), notifications and follows (M4-F64), work times through delete_work_times_in (M8-F30), agents and standing rules (M7-F36, M9-Q5); their project memberships end, while issues assigned to them stay assigned, shown as Former user, for somebody to change. One table in bb-core (removal.rs) says, for each kind of record, what the person is to a row that goes, and every kind it does not name is kept (amended 2026-11-19 with what the code deletes):
      • a row goes where the person holds it or is its subject (their own sign-in, keys, grants, handle, settings, follows, the rows that give them roles and the members of groups they are in), where they wrote it as its only author (private saved searches, drafts, standing rules) or where they are its recipient (notifications, notes of an edit). A notification or a note of an edit the person caused for somebody else stays with that person, shown as Former user;
      • invitations, used or open, that the person made or got: sign-in records of the account, which tell nothing to the organization once the account is gone;
      • files of Download my data made of the person: the plan names them in words of their own, saying that a file not fetched yet goes too, so an administrator gives it to the person first;
      • hand-overs the person made: each gives work to one of the person's own agents, which go too; the agent work they started stays as a record of the issue, shown as Former user;
      • away times: they belong to work times and go with them through delete_work_times_in. Their keep period of one year (ADR-0045) is a longest time, not a time the law asks for, so it keeps nothing past the removal; work days, which the law keeps, are a kind of their own and stay;
    • makes the person a tombstone with the code that bb-policy's former_user_label draws (no second way to draw it), stored as the FormerUser label that Target.removed carries, so every reference shows Former user … through PersonRef::Former;
    • clears the name and the e-mail address from the person's record. When the person has work days inside their keep period, the name moves into one legal-hold field of the tombstone, with its reason ("work days, ArbZG §16") and its end (the date of the last kept work day plus the keep period). resolve reads that field, and only for the working-hours context it already serves. The field is cleared in the change in which an administrator's Delete them (ADR-0045) deletes the person's last work days; no job clears it. Time entries do not keep the name: they show Former user like everything else (M9-Q6);
    • scrubs the copies of personal values in the events: the before and after of the person's own settings (M2-F75), the name and text of their private searches (M5-F63), and the values that the deleted rows carried; the changes the person made to records only their owner makes (whose::MADE_ONLY_BY_THEIR_OWNER: access keys, passkeys, connected AI apps, sessions), even when the record is gone; and every value that holds their full name as one phrase of whole words (a name of two words or more; a name of one word, such as "Mark", is a common word too often and is found through the person's mentions and address), one of their handles as a mention (@ and the whole handle, the only way a handle stands in a text), or their address anywhere, capitals not counting and in any script. The database picks the rows that may hold a name by the letters of ASCII it folds like Rust; a name with none of them (Cyrillic, Greek, Chinese) makes the scrub read the events, the history and the notifications in full, by key in pages, while it holds the write lock of SQLite (measured at the exit of M9, M9-F51). What the person did to the records of others (the roles they gave, the work times they edited) keeps its values;
    • leaves the work days, their breaks and reasons, and the security log, whose entries name the person by ID and so read Former user … from then on.

    What cannot be done inside one change (the full-text index of the texts that change, with SQLite's secure_delete on the segments, M5-F52) is a job, privacy.finish-removal, queued in that change and safe to run again. On PostgreSQL only the reindex runs: no step a job can take makes VACUUM overwrite the old rows, so the database's own vacuum takes the space back in its time. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-PERSON-REF, ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-DB-PARITY (the removal tests on both databases).

  7. Texts the person wrote (M9-Q3): the window offers Keep their comments, shown as Former user (the start, an organization setting privacy.removed-texts) or Delete their comments. Issue descriptions, fields, time entries and files they made are business records of the organization and stay, shown as Former user; deleting them is the ordinary deletion of each. Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX, review (no other text is deleted by the choice).

  8. The replay list: what a restore must not undo (M9-Q11). Every removal (with its choice about comments), every switch-off, and every taking back of an access key, an AI app grant, a passkey or a support access writes one line to privacy/replay.list in the data folder: the kind, the ID, the moment, and for a removal the comments choice; no name and no other value. After a restore from an older backup, the restore runs every line newer than the backup again before the server opens (ADR-0046). A replayed removal does not ask for the switch-off first, and it applies the comments choice of its line, so deleted comments do not come back. Switch on writes no line: a restore that runs an earlier switch-off again leaves the person switched off, which fails safe, and an administrator switches them on again. A line names no administrator, so the standing of a line run again names nobody as who did it (by is empty: a restore did it; migration 60 lets the column be empty and empties any row that names the person themselves), and a replayed removal draws a new Former user label, because the line holds none; references show the new label from then on. A replay does not ask whether somebody still decides roles; when the lines it ran leave nobody who does, the restore says so in its report and in the security log, and setup is open again. A line is written in the change it stands for, into the database, and moves into the file right after the commit; a line the file does not take waits there, goes with the next write and before every backup, and the security log says that it waits. The list is kept in three places that a restore merges: the data folder, a copy inside every backup, and the copy that bugaboo keys export writes beside the keys, so a computer lost with its data folder does not lose the list. Enforced by: review (the restore tests of ADR-0046 cover each kind of line).

  9. Corrections (PRIV-06): a person corrects their own name; a change of their e-mail address takes effect when they open a link sent to the new address, and the old address is told. An administrator with Manage people corrects the name and e-mail address of others with a reason; the person is told, and the security log records it. Other personal data already has its own way to be corrected (work days with a reason, ADR-0035; work times, ADR-0030). Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-EVENTS.

Consequences

  • A new entity that names a person has to declare its links, or the build fails, so export and removal cannot forget it. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS.
  • The tombstone keeps every reference valid: history, comments and issues still read, with Former user … where a name was.
  • The only place a removed person's name survives is the legal-hold field, with a reason and an end date that the removal window shows.
  • Removal is not undone. The window says so, and the plan is shown before anything happens.
  • Backups older than a removal still hold the person until their keep period ends; the keep rule Backups (ADR-0045) bounds that time, and the replay list stops a restore from bringing the person back.

Alternatives considered

  • Each feature writes its own export and removal code: the exact failure ADR-0015 was written to avoid. Rejected.
  • Overwrite the person's ID in every row: breaks the security log's chain and every foreign key, and gains nothing over a tombstone whose name and e-mail are gone. Rejected.
  • Keep the whole person row while work days are held: keeps the e-mail address and the rest for years for the one field the law needs. Rejected in favour of one legal-hold field.
  • Delete everything the person wrote: destroys the organization's records (issues, decisions, time booked for customers) that it may keep under Art. 17(3). Rejected; the choice covers comments only.
  • Export synchronously in the request: a person with years of work produces a large file; a job keeps the server responsive. Rejected.

Enforced by

DATA-MARKS, ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-PERSON-REF, ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-DB-PARITY, DATA-LOGS; review (the one walk, the legal-hold field, and what a replay restores).

Amendment (M9, how corrections are kept)

  • One keyed digest. The secret of the link to a new address, the memory of sign-up e-mails (M4-F122) and the values a correction replaces are kept as an HMAC-SHA256 under a key of the server (bb_auth::DigestKey). It is the same key as keys/csrf.key, kept apart by a name: every digest starts with a name of its own, as every signed link does, so there is no further key file to back up or rotate: what depends on it lives an hour or is only ever compared. Enforced by: review (one function makes every keyed digest).
  • What the history keeps. A person's own new name is kept in the history in clear, as the change of a short value. A change of an address keeps only the keyed digests of both addresses, and a correction by an administrator keeps the keyed digests of the old and the new value and the reason. The security log names who changed what of whom and holds no value. Enforced by: review (the tests priv_06_* check the events).
  • The second check of a new address asks for the password again; a passkey as the second check comes later (M9-F80). The link to a new address is made like the link of an invitation (OneUseLink, one hour, one use), and the daily job sessions.purge deletes the links that ran out (the row Links that confirm a new e-mail address of ADR-0045).

ADR-0045: Keep and delete rules

Status: Accepted · 2026-11-18 · refines PRIV-05, ADR-0017 and ADR-0035 decision 7; the answers to M9-Q1 and M9-Q2 of the M9 plan

Context

PRIV-05 asks for "keep and delete rules per kind of data … with automatic deletion" and sensible defaults. UX design §5.7 draws one table: working hours, time on issues, the security log, IP addresses, notifications, the trash.

Some of it exists, scattered. The security log is pruned by a daily job after security.log-keep-days; notifications go after 90 days; dead sessions, drafts, OAuth grants and away times have daily jobs; the files of the trash go after 30 days. Work days are never deleted by Bugaboo: after their keep period an administrator deletes them, a decision of the maintainer (ADR-0035, decision 7). Issues in the trash stay for ever (M3-F25, M4-F131), and so do the events that carry old values (M4-F93, M6-F45), the payload of dead jobs (M1-F21) and the lines of the security log's anchor file (M1-F26).

The maintainer's rule is that a keep period is a minimum: as long as data is relevant to the organization, keeping it is legitimate, and only the organization can judge relevance. So business records are never deleted by Bugaboo by itself. Data that only serves a technical purpose, or that protects a person, has no such interest behind it and should go by itself.

Decision

  1. Two kinds of rule (M9-Q1). Every kind of data has one row in one list, keeping::KEEP_KINDS in bb-core, and each row is one of:

    • Deleted by itself after its period: data with no business purpose of its own. IP addresses in logs (7 days), sessions and sign-in history (90 days after they end), sign-up links, drafts, notifications (90 days), the trash (30 days, which finishes a deletion a person already made; an issue whose time entries are still inside their keep period stays in the trash, hidden, until the last of them leaves it, so the purge never takes a business record along, M9-Q1), data exports (7 days), the payload of dead jobs (30 days), away times (1 year after their last day, ADR-0030), the security log (1 year, in whole blocks, ADR-0007), backups (by their schedule, ADR-0046), and, from M14, the record of an ended support access (with the security log's period, ADR-0048).
    • Deleted by an administrator after its period: business records. Work days with their breaks and reasons (at least 2 years with the preset Germany, ADR-0035) and time entries (10 years at the start, M9-Q2: German law keeps receipts 8 years since 2025 and the books 10, and Bugaboo cannot tell which entries are which). Bugaboo shows how many are past the period and offers Delete them, as it does for work days today.

    Enforced by: ARCH-SETTINGS (each period is a setting of the registry), review (a new kind of business record joins the second group; a job that deletes one is a finding).

  2. One page shows them all. Organization settings › Privacy › Keep and delete rules lists every row of KEEP_KINDS, with its period, what happens then, and why, in plain words. A period is changed there; a change that would delete something at once first says how much ("312 notifications will be deleted tonight"). The table of the user docs is written from the same list. Enforced by: DOC-GENERATED (the table of the user docs), ARCH-SETTINGS.

  3. A period cannot go below its floor. Each row has a lowest period: the law's for records the law asks for (work days, ADR-0035), a technical floor for the rest (the trash at least 1 day, so a deletion can still be undone). Enforced by: ARCH-SETTINGS (the registry refuses a value below the floor), review (each floor names its reason).

  4. Records take their events along. When a record is deleted, by a job or by an administrator, the events that carry its values go in the same change (ADR-0007): the domain event of an upload with its file name (M4-F93), the note and fields of a time entry (M6-F45), the reasons of a work day (as today). The history of a record that still exists is kept. Enforced by: ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-DB-PARITY.

  5. One way to delete by itself. Every row of the first group is a daily kind of JobKind (rhythm FromTheStart, or QuietHour for the large ones) that deletes in steps of KEEP_STEP_ROWS rows, one short write each, so a write of people never waits long behind it (M4-F104). The existing jobs move under this one shape; no second loop of deleting is written. The security log's anchor file is trimmed by the same job that prunes the log, keeping the newest line and writing the trimmed file next to the old one before it is renamed into place (M1-F26). Enforced by: ARCH-EVENTS, PERF-N1, review (one helper for deleting in steps).

  6. One way for an administrator to delete. The count of what is past its period and Delete them work the same for every row of the second group, through one use case (the one that deletes old work days today becomes general). It needs Change organization settings, no key or agent can call it, and every run writes how many of what (and of whom) were deleted to the security log, each step in the same change as what it deleted, so a run that stops between steps leaves nothing deleted without its entry. A run that deletes the last kept work days of a removed person clears that person's legal-hold name in the same change (ADR-0044, decision 6). Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-EVENTS.

Consequences

  • Some rows of UX design §5.7 change: Time on issues reads "10 years, then an administrator deletes them" instead of "Deleted" (M9-Q2).
  • The keep periods of a removed person's records come from the same list, so the window of Remove a person (ADR-0044) says "kept until 2028-10-01" from it.
  • Every kind of data an upcoming feature adds (documents, M11) needs a row; a missing row is a finding.

Alternatives considered

  • Automatic deletion for everything, as PRIV-05 first said: the maintainer decided that business records are deleted only explicitly (M6, ADR-0035); doing it for some records and not others by accident is worse. Rejected.
  • Nothing deleted by itself: keeps IP addresses, sessions and exports far longer than any purpose needs (Art. 5(1)(e) GDPR). Rejected.
  • A rule per project: nobody asked, and it multiplies the questions of Remove a person. Not now.

Enforced by

ARCH-SETTINGS, ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-DB-PARITY, PERF-N1, DOC-GENERATED; review (which group a new kind of data joins).

Amendment (M9, who reads the rules and what a change would delete)

  • Every person reads the rules. GET /api/v1/admin/keep-rules answers every person who signs in with a session, not an access key or an agent: how long their data is kept is part of what GDPR Art. 15(1)(d) gives them, and My settings › My data shows it. The answer is the same for everybody, the setting and the floor of each row included, because a keep period is not secret. Changing a period and the counts stay with Change organization settings. Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX.
  • What a changed period would delete is counted with the cutoff of the deleting. GET /api/v1/admin/keep-rules/{kind}/would-delete?count=… counts, before a period is saved, the records the job of a kind of the first group would delete with the changed period, or the records of a kind of the second group that would be past it. The settings as they would be come from KeepRule::with_period, the cutoff from the same function as the job's (keep_cutoff_with, kept_from_today_with), and each count from the condition the purge of its kind deletes by (bb-store, keeping/past.rs), so the count and the deleting cannot drift apart. Only a kind whose period is one setting has a count: a fixed period is never changed, and the rotation of backups is the work of two settings on the page of backups. Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-DB-PARITY (the counts on both databases), review (no second cutoff).

ADR-0046: Backups, restore and upgrades

Status: Accepted · 2026-11-18 · refines OPS-06, OPS-07, ADR-0003 and the upgrade line of architecture §6; the answers to M9-Q9 to M9-Q11 of the M9 plan

Context

OPS-07 asks for online backup and restore, from the command line and from the screens, with scheduled backups and retention. OPS-06 asks that an upgrade migrates the database by itself, makes a backup first, and has a clear way back. Architecture §6 already promises it: "on start, Bugaboo makes a backup, then runs migrations; if a migration fails, it restores the backup and stops with a plain explanation". None of it is built: the data folder has an empty backups/, and migrations run at start with no copy made.

A backup of Bugaboo is more than the database: the files of attachments live in files/, the master key and the log key in keys/, and the security log is anchored in logs/security-head.log, outside the database. A restore of an older database leaves the anchor ahead of it, and the status page then stays at "problem" with no way out (M2-F09). A restore of a backup older than a Remove a person, a switch-off or a key taken back would bring them back (ADR-0044).

Bugaboo runs on SQLite (the start) and PostgreSQL. Both have to be backed up while people work.

Decision

  1. One backup is one file (M9-Q9): bugaboo-<moment>-<version>.backup in backups/ (or a folder the administrator names), a tar archive with a manifest (manifest.json: the version of Bugaboo, the set of applied migrations with their checksums, the database kind, the moment, the head of the security log, and the SHA-256 of every member), the database, the files of attachments that the database points to, and a copy of the replay list (ADR-0044, decision 8). A backup holds no keys: whoever restores it on another computer brings the keys with bugaboo keys export and keys import, and a restore checks that the master key opens the stored secrets before it goes on. Enforced by: review (the manifest is the one description of a backup), DATA-LOGS.

  2. The database is copied while people work. SQLite: VACUUM INTO a file of the backup's temporary folder, which reads one consistent state; writers do not wait for it, but the write-ahead log grows while the copy runs and is checkpointed after it. PostgreSQL: Bugaboo's own copy, table by table in one transaction at REPEATABLE READ, written in the order of the migrations, so no outside program (pg_dump) and no fixed path is needed (coding-standards §2). A restore goes into the same kind of database. Enforced by: ARCH-DB-PARITY (the backup and restore tests on both databases), LINT-PATHS.

  3. Making a backup. bugaboo backup (to the folder of the settings, or --to <folder>), the button Make a backup now in Organization settings › System › Backups (with Change organization settings), and the schedule: daily at the quiet hour (backups.daily, on at the start), keeping the newest 7 daily and 4 weekly backups (backups.keep-daily, backups.keep-weekly). Every backup writes one line to the security log with its name and checksum. A backup that fails is an alert on the status page and a notification to administrators. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS, ARCH-SETTINGS, SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-EVENTS.

  4. Restoring from the command line (M9-Q10 and M9-Q20). bugaboo restore <file> runs with the server stopped, and the page Backups shows that command; a restore from the screen is not part of the MVP (OPS-07 as reworded). A restore:

    • checks every checksum of the manifest and refuses a backup of a newer version or a damaged one, changing nothing;
    • makes a backup of what is there now first, so a restore can itself be undone; that backup is kept out of the rotation for the keep period of the security log, because it is the evidence of what the restore replaced;
    • signs everybody out, the command line's restore included (every session of the restored database ends);
    • puts the database and the files back, runs the migrations of a backup from an older version (decision 5), merges the copies of the replay list (the data folder's, the backup's and one given with --replay-list) and runs every line newer than the backup (ADR-0044, decision 8: removals, switch-offs, keys, grants, passkeys and support accesses taken back);
    • verifies the restored security log, writes the head it reached to the anchor file as a new start with the lost range named, and writes a security-log entry that says what was restored and which entries after the backup's head are gone (M2-F09). The restore's report lists what the replay did again, and says that every other change after the backup's moment is gone, password and role changes included, so the administrator can tell the people concerned.

    Enforced by: ARCH-DB-PARITY (the restore tests on both databases), ARCH-EVENTS.

  5. Upgrades back up first. When the server starts and the set of migrations applied to the database lacks some of the program's, the server makes a backup (decision 1) before the first migration, named before-<version>, and keeps it outside the rotation of decision 3; the newest three such backups are kept (backups.keep-before-upgrade), older ones go with the rotation. If a migration fails, the server restores that backup, stops, and says in plain words what failed, where the backup is, and that the previous program works with it. A database with a migration the program does not know is refused, as today. The migrations of a release can only be checked against a real older database, so every release is tested by upgrading a database made by the previous milestone's program (the upgrade test, WP-07). Enforced by: DATA-MIGRATIONS, ARCH-DB-PARITY, review (the upgrade test runs before a release).

  6. Where the files go. Backups are as private as the data folder (owner only, at every start, M1-F65). Backups are not encrypted in the MVP; encryption with the master key is SEC-20 (V1). The page Backups says where they are and that they hold all the organization's data. Enforced by: review (the data-folder tests of sec_16_… cover backups/).

Consequences

  • Keys are backed up apart from data, on purpose: a stolen backup does not carry the key that opens its secrets.
  • A restore is an event in the security log, and the chain explains the gap instead of breaking.
  • Every release costs one more test: a database made by the program of the previous milestone, upgraded.

Alternatives considered

  • pg_dump and sqlite3 as outside programs: extra installs, versions that must match the server, and a path to find. Rejected.
  • The keys inside the backup: one file restores everything, but whoever holds the file holds every secret. Rejected until backups are encrypted (SEC-20, V1).
  • Restore from the screen in M9, as OPS-07 first said: many administrators never open a console on the server, but the screen needs a restore mode, a second check and its own concurrency tests for an action that is rare and done with the service stopped. Not in the MVP (M9-Q20); a later milestone may add it on top of this record.
  • A folder per backup instead of one file: easier to read, harder to move and to check whole. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-DB-PARITY, DATA-MIGRATIONS, ARCH-PERMS, ARCH-SETTINGS, ARCH-EVENTS, SEC-MATRIX, LINT-PATHS, DATA-LOGS; review (the manifest, and the upgrade test before each release).

Amendment: a backup is sealed with the keys of its installation

The security review of the first build found that a restore took any backup file whose checksums matched its manifest, so a file that somebody else wrote, for example one whose database plants an administrator, would be restored, and that a master key of another installation passed when the backup held no stored secret. Decision 1 is refined:

  • The seal. Every backup carries manifest.seal right after manifest.json: an HMAC-SHA256 of the exact bytes of the manifest under the log key of the installation, which never changes. The manifest names the SHA-256 of every other member, so the seal covers the whole backup. A restore checks it before it writes any member and refuses a backup without it, or with one its keys did not make, changing nothing. A backup of another installation is restored after its key files are imported (bugaboo keys import).
  • The check values of the master keys. The manifest lists, for each master key of the installation, its ID and an HMAC of a fixed text under it. A restore refuses a master key of the same ID with another check value, and keys that share no ID with the backup, before anything is replaced, whether or not the backup holds stored secrets.
  • Each HMAC starts with a text of its own, so neither can stand for the other or for a signature of the security log under the same key. The backup still holds no key (decision 1): an HMAC shows whether a key is the same key, not the key.

Enforced by: the restore tests ops_07_a_backup_another_installation_sealed_is_refused_before_anything_is_replaced and ops_07_a_wrong_master_key_stops_the_restore_before_anything_is_replaced (both databases), and the archive test ops_07_a_backup_this_installation_did_not_seal_is_refused.

Amendment: the backup before an upgrade, as built

Building the upgrade showed where decision 5 had to be exact. Decision 5 is refined:

  • The name. The backup is bugaboo-before-upgrade-<moment>-<version>.backup, with the version of the program that makes it, in the format of decision 1.
  • The folder. It always goes into backups/ of the data folder, never into a folder the administrator named for the other backups: that folder is a setting in the database, and the settings may not be readable before the migrations have run.
  • How many are kept. The newest N are kept, N being backups.keep-before-upgrade (3 at the start); the rotation of decision 3 deletes older ones, in backups/ of the data folder whatever folder the other backups go into.
  • version.txt in the data folder exists only for the words of a stop: it holds the version of the program that last started on the data, so the words can name the previous version, and, from the backup to the end of the migrations, the name of the backup made before them. A start after one that was cut off part way then says that the database may be half changed, tells the administrator not to start Bugaboo on it, names that backup (while it is there) to be kept, and does not say that the previous program works with the database. Going back from it needs a restore that does not migrate (M9-F62).
  • The stop. Every start that stops at an upgrade (a newer database, a migration this program does not have, or has in another form, a backup that failed, a migration that failed) exits with UPGRADE_STOPPED = 65, defined once in crates/bb-server/src/upgrade.rs; a Windows service reports it as its own service-specific code, so a service manager can tell that starting again does not help.

Enforced by: TEST-UPGRADE, DATA-MIGRATIONS, ARCH-DB-PARITY.

ADR-0047: Releases: signatures, the parts list, the support period and vulnerability handling

Status: Accepted · 2026-11-18 · refines SEC-18, COMP-01, COMP-03, COMP-04, DIST-07 and ADR-0040; the answers to M9-Q12 to M9-Q14 and M9-Q16 of the M9 plan

Context

M9 ends with the first release of Bugaboo that people can install and run for real. The Cyber Resilience Act asks a manufacturer for a software bill of materials, a way to report vulnerabilities, advisories, reports of actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 and 72 hours (in force since 11 September 2026), free security updates for a declared support period, and secure defaults (compliance.md §1). The new Product Liability Directive covers software placed on the market from 9 December 2026. Bugaboo is free, AGPL-licensed, and nothing commercial is offered until a lawyer has reviewed it (ADR-0036, decision 5).

Today the repository has lockfiles, the register of direct dependencies, the license allow list and the advisory scan (DEP-REGISTER, DEP-LICENSES, SEC-ADVISORIES), SECURITY.md with private reporting on GitHub, and cargo xtask build, which builds the Windows program. DEP-SBOM is planned and not built. Nothing is signed. There is no certificate for Windows code signing on this computer, no hosted build (ADR-0037), and the static Linux program is built only on Linux.

Decision

  1. What a release is. A release is a tag vX.Y.Z on main, the version of ADR-0040 (M9 brings 0.6.0). cargo xtask release builds it on the development PC and in WSL and writes one folder: the programs (decision 7), SHA256SUMS, a signature for each file, the parts list (decision 3), the third-party notices, the release notes and known issues. The maintainer publishes that folder as a GitHub release and as the files a served instance is updated from. Enforced by: DEP-SBOM, review (the maintainer publishes).

  2. Signatures with our own key (M9-Q12). Every file of a release, the checksum list and the parts list are signed with one Ed25519 release key in the minisign format, so anybody can check them with that common tool or with bugaboo update verify <file>, which knows the public key. The public keys are written once, as a list (bb-core::release::RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEYS): the release key and a backup key that the maintainer keeps apart, so a lost or leaked key can be replaced by a release signed with the other; the rotation is a written step of the release guide. They are copied into SECURITY.md and the release page by the build. The program verifies with minisign-verify; xtask signs with minisign; both get their register rows. The private key never enters the repository or a work folder: the maintainer keeps it offline with a passphrase and signs with cargo xtask release sign. Tests sign with a key made for the test. Windows code signing (Authenticode) waits for a certificate the maintainer decides on; until then Windows warns about an unknown publisher, and the install guide says how to check the signature first. Enforced by: SEC-SECRETS (no key in the repository), review (the signing step reads the key from outside the work folder).

  3. The parts list (SBOM; decided by the rules: one source, no new tool). cargo xtask release writes it in CycloneDX 1.6 JSON and SPDX 2.3 JSON from the lockfiles (single source, coding-standards §1): every crate that is compiled into each program (the dependency tree of the target, without build-only and test-only crates), every npm package bundled into the browser app, and the texts of docs/third-party/notices/, each with version, license and checksum. Bugaboo bundles no font files (it uses the system font stacks); the Lucide icons (ISC) are listed as the package or files they come from. xtask writes both formats itself from cargo metadata and package-lock.json; no new tool is installed; a test-only JSON schema validator of xtask checks both files. The program carries the parts list and the notices of its own build, so About shows them. Enforced by: DEP-SBOM (made, complete against the lockfiles, valid against both schemas), DEP-REGISTER, DEP-LICENSES.

  4. Vulnerability handling.

    • SECURITY.md says which versions get fixes (decision 5), how to report (GitHub's private reporting), the answer within one week, coordinated disclosure within 90 days, and that we report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents through ENISA's single reporting platform within 24 hours (early warning), 72 hours (notification) and the final report.
    • The runbook docs/security/vulnerability-runbook.md lists the steps from report to advisory, with the CRA deadlines; the full incident runbook for us as manufacturer and operator is DIST-08 (V1).
    • Every advisory that is accepted in deny.toml or tools/checks/npm-advisories.toml gets a VEX statement in the release folder (CycloneDX VEX: not affected and why), written from the same entries and the register's Accepted risks, so the reason is written once (M6-F126).
    • Bugaboo serves /.well-known/security.txt (RFC 9116, M9-Q16): our contact first, the organization's own contact when an administrator sets one, and an expiry one year after the release, so an old installation shows its age.

    Enforced by: SEC-ADVISORIES, DEP-SBOM, SEC-HEADERS, review (the runbook is read before each release).

  5. The support period (M9-Q13). Until 1.0, every release is a free public preview: only the newest release gets fixes, and a fix comes as the next patch release (0.6.1). From 1.0 on, each minor release gets security fixes for 5 years from its date, declared on the release page and in About. Security fixes ship as patch releases made from the release's tag on a branch release-X.Y, without new features. Enforced by: review (the release notes name the support period).

  6. Secure by default (COMP-04). The settings that matter for security start safe and a test lists them: HTTPS on, sign-up off, every kind of AI off, e-mail off, outside images blocked, two-step sign-in offered, the data folder owner-only. docs/security/cra-requirements.md maps each essential requirement of the CRA (Annex I) to the features, checks and tests that meet it. Enforced by: ARCH-SETTINGS, SEC-HEADERS, review (the mapping is read before each release).

  7. Platforms of the first release (decided by the rules): Windows x64 and Linux x64 (static, for any distribution and WSL). Windows ARM64 waits for the ARM64 build tools (M1-F01), Linux ARM64 for a cross linker; both join a later release without a change to the code. Enforced by: review (the release folder lists its platforms).

  8. Updates (DIST-07; M9-Q14). A self-hosted installation is updated by replacing the program after the installed program's bugaboo update verify <new file> has checked the new file's signature and warned when the version in its trusted comment is older than its own (a downgrade); the next start backs up and migrates (ADR-0046). The update notice inside Bugaboo and its signed check of the feed are OPS-11 (V1, M14). Served instances are updated by us with the same signed files, in announced maintenance windows, from M14 (DIST-02). Enforced by: review (the install guide and the release notes describe the update).

Consequences

  • A release needs the maintainer twice: to sign with the offline key, and to publish.
  • A person on Windows sees a warning about an unknown publisher until a code-signing certificate is bought (M9-Q12).
  • The parts list is checked in every full run, not only at release time, so a release never finds a gap late.

Amendment (M9, the parts list)

  • The schema validator is a normal dependency of xtask, not a development-only one. Decision 3 said "test-only". The check DEP-SBOM runs inside the xtask program in every full run and must validate both files, so the validator (jsonschema, built without its network code) is compiled into xtask. It is never part of the program that ships, and its register row says so. Enforced by: DEP-REGISTER.
  • The crate list is what cargo tree -e normal says each program compiles in. cargo metadata joins the features of every member of the workspace, so it names crates that a program does not compile in; it still gives the licenses and the edges. DEP-SBOM holds the list to cargo tree in both directions, and the npm packages to the lockfile's own marks (not dev, not devOptional). Enforced by: DEP-SBOM.
  • A crate without a license file gets the standard text of its declared license in the notices (decision 3), with the authors named in the package as the copyright holders.
  • The VEX reason is the register's. A statement takes its reason and its CycloneDX justification from the row of the register's Accepted risks; an accepted advisory without a row, or with a justification CycloneDX does not know, fails DEP-SBOM. Enforced by: DEP-SBOM.
  • The files are the same bytes only for the same lockfiles and the same installed packages: the license texts are read from the installed crates and packages.

Amendment (M9, signed releases and the support period)

  • The trusted comment of every signature is file:<name> and version:<version>, separated by a tab like the comments of the minisign tool (bb_core::release::TrustedComment, one writer and one reader). Only signatures of the file's hash (the minisign default) are taken. bugaboo update verify checks the file's signature, the signature of SHA256SUMS beside it, and the file's checksum in that list under the name its signature gives, so a download saved under another name is still found. Enforced by: review (sec_18_…, dist_07_…).
  • Where the support period lives. [workspace.metadata.release] of Cargo.toml holds the day of the release and the years of support from 1.0; bb_core::release reads it at compile time, so a missing or malformed entry stops the build. A preview (0.x) answers fixes_until: null in About. security.txt expires one year after that day. Enforced by: review (comp_04_about_answers_the_support_period_from_its_one_home).
  • Test keys until the real ones. RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEYS holds two test keys whose secret keys were thrown away, and KEYS_ARE_FOR_TESTS is true; SECURITY.md and the notes say so. The change that puts the real keys in sets it to false. Enforced by: DOC-GENERATED (SECURITY.md follows the code).
  • The organization's contact (security.contact) is taken only as one https:// address or e-mail address (made into mailto:): anything else is refused when it is saved, with a sentence that says what to write, and left out of security.txt should a database hold it, so a value can never add a field. Enforced by: review (comp_03_…).
  • The secure defaults (decision 6) are one table in the test comp_04_every_setting_that_matters_for_security_starts_safe. Every setting of sign-in, security, AI, AI apps, agents, the assistant, e-mail, content and files is judged there: it is in the table with its starting value, or in a list of settings that do not matter for security, with the reason; a new one fails the test until it is in one of them. Every kind of AI starts off: the assistant, AI apps and agents (ai-apps.enabled and agents.enabled start off; this replaces the on of ADR-0029 and ADR-0042). A stored value is only a change of the default, so the change alone would switch both off in every installation that never touched them: migration 59 writes on as the organization's own value where a person already exists and the organization set no value, so an upgrade keeps AI apps and agents as they were, and a new installation, which migrates before setup makes the first person, starts with both off. Enforced by: ARCH-SETTINGS, the tests comp_04_… of migration 59 on both databases, review.
  • The release name of a test build. A folder built without its tag on the commit, or while KEYS_ARE_FOR_TESTS is true, is named <version>-test, and so is every file in it and the version in every trusted comment, so a signed test file never passes for a release. Once the real keys are in, release sign refuses a folder built without its tag and a key that is not in RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEYS, and cargo xtask release refuses a day of the release that is not the day of the tag's commit. release check names a file in the folder that does not belong there. bugaboo update verify takes SHA256SUMS only when its signature names file:SHA256SUMS and the same version as the file. Enforced by: review (sec_18_…).
  • The support period counts from X.Y.0 (decision 5): [workspace.metadata.release] holds minor-date, the day of the first release of the minor version, beside date; a patch release never adds time. Enforced by: review (comp_04_a_patch_release_is_supported_from_the_day_of_its_minor_release).

Alternatives considered

  • Sigstore (cosign keyless): needs a hosted build identity and the network at signing time; ADR-0037 has no hosted build. Not now.
  • GPG signatures: heavier for people to check, with key servers and trust models. Rejected in favour of minisign's single public key.
  • cargo cyclonedx and @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm: two more pinned tools that each cover half and still need merging; SPDX needs a third. Rejected.
  • 5 years of support for 0.x: a promise a single maintainer cannot keep for previews, and a preview is not placed on the market commercially. Rejected until 1.0.

Enforced by

DEP-SBOM, DEP-REGISTER, DEP-LICENSES, SEC-ADVISORIES, SEC-SECRETS, SEC-HEADERS, ARCH-SETTINGS; review (signing, publishing and the runbook are steps of the maintainer).

ADR-0048: Support access with the customer's approval

Status: Accepted in part · 2026-11-18 · decision 1 holds from M9 on; decisions 2 to 6 are planned for M14, with DIST-03, which became a V1 feature (M9-Q20) · refines DIST-03, ADR-0012 and boundary 4 of architecture §12; the answers to M9-Q15 and M9-Q20 of the M9 plan

Context

DIST-03 says that our staff have no access to customer data by default, and that emergency access happens only with the customer's approval, time-limited, and recorded in the customer's own security log. Architecture §6 sketches it for the served model: "an operator requests access; the customer's administrator approves in their own Bugaboo".

The served model and its control plane come in M14. But the need comes earlier: a self-hosted customer who asks us for help with their installation makes us their processor for that support case (compliance.md §5), and the same rules apply. What can be built now is the customer's side: a way for an administrator to let one named supporter in, for a short time, with limited rights, seen by everybody who reads the security log, and ended at any moment.

Decision

Decision 1 is in force from M9. Decisions 2 to 6 are the plan for M14 and are reviewed there with the served model before they are built.

  1. Nothing by default. Bugaboo has no built-in account, key or back door for us or anybody else, in either model. Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX (no route answers without a session or key that the organization made), ARCH-SETTINGS (the test of secure defaults of M9 lists no account but the first administrator's), review (no account is made outside an invitation, and in M14 Support access).
  2. Support access is a time-limited account the administrator makes (M9-Q15). In Organization settings › System › Support access an administrator with Change organization settings names the supporter (a name and an e-mail address), a reason, a role (any role that holds no permission the administrator lacks; the start is Viewer), the projects it counts in, and an end (at most 72 hours, support-access.longest; the start is 8 hours). Bugaboo shows a one-time link, good for one hour, which the administrator passes on. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS, ARCH-SETTINGS, SEC-MATRIX.
  3. The supporter signs in with two steps. Opening the link sets a password and a code app or passkey before anything else; there is no access key, no AI app grant and no agent for such an account. Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-AI-TOOLS.
  4. Everything is in the customer's security log. The making, each sign-in, every request of the supporter (not only changes: route and record, never the content), and the end. The requests are appended one after another like every write (M1-F23), and their number is bounded by the API's limit per client (rate_limit_per_minute), so a supporter cannot slow the others more than any client can. People see a support account as "Sam Lee (support access until 18:00)" wherever a person is named. Enforced by: ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-PERSON-REF.
  5. It ends by itself and on demand. At its end, or when any administrator chooses End now, the sessions end at once and the account is removed as in Remove a person (ADR-0044), keeping its security-log entries. The record of the access (supporter's name, reason, role, places, start, end, maker) is kept for the keep period of the security log, then deleted by that keep rule (ADR-0045), so a log entry can always be read with who and why. A job checks every minute so no session outlives its end by more than that. Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX (a request one minute after the end is refused), ARCH-EVENTS.
  6. The served model later uses the same door. In M14 the control plane may ask for support access through the operator API (DIST-02); the customer's administrator still makes it here, under the same rules. The control plane never holds a way in of its own. Enforced by: review (M14 builds on this record and does not add a second way).

Consequences

  • Until M14, a self-hosted customer who wants help invites a supporter with a role and removes them afterwards; both are in the security log. From M14, support access gives that a safe, time-limited shape.
  • Every support case is visible to the customer afterwards, request by request.
  • The supporter's work is limited to what the administrator chose, and Bugaboo, not trust, keeps it there.

Alternatives considered

  • A shared support password or a built-in support account: a back door. Rejected.
  • Screen sharing only: works and needs no feature, but leaves no record in Bugaboo and lets the supporter see whatever is on the screen. Kept as the customer's own choice, outside Bugaboo.
  • Build all of it in M9: DIST-03 was an MVP feature, but the operators it is for come with the served model, and M9 was too large. The maintainer moved decisions 2 to 6 to M14 (M9-Q20).

Enforced by

SEC-MATRIX, ARCH-PERMS, ARCH-SETTINGS, ARCH-AI-TOOLS, ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-PERSON-REF; review (no second way in).
